meta.title: Mammoth Energy Services — TUSK's pivot from oilfield pressure pumping to electric T&D and data center infrastructure
meta.abstract: Mammoth Energy Services, Inc. (NASDAQ: TUSK) is a Oklahoma City-headquartered diversified services company spun out of Wexford Capital-backed assets. Three principal segments: (1) Infrastructure Services — transmission and distribution (T&D) line construction, substation work, and increasingly data center electrical infrastructure through subsidiary 5 Star Electric and related entities, with historical Cobra Acquisitions exposure to the post-Hurricane-Maria Puerto Rico T&D rebuild; (2) Oilfield Services — pressure pumping, well completion, and related services historically branded under brands like Wexford-affiliated pumping, with significant cyclical decline through 2020-2023; (3) Natural Sand Proppant — frac sand mining and logistics. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 centered on the data center electrical infrastructure pivot driven by AI buildout demand for grid-tied capacity, alongside ongoing PREPA Puerto Rico arbitration/litigation overhang and the broader transition away from declining oilfield exposure.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## Pivot Arrested

Mammoth Energy Services enters the summer of 2026 as a company whose strategic narrative has been overtaken by its own transactions. Listed on NASDAQ under the ticker TUSK and headquartered in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, the company had been cast through much of 2024 as a candidate beneficiary of the AI-driven data-centre buildout — its Infrastructure Services subsidiaries, including 5 Star Electric and Cobra Acquisitions, positioned to wire the power-hungry compute clusters reshaping the US grid. By April 2025, those subsidiaries were gone, sold to Peak Utility Services Group for $108.7 million. The chief executive who had arrived to execute the infrastructure strategy departed with them. Mammoth is now a materially different entity: a post-settlement cash box anchored by aviation auxiliary-power-unit rentals, residual frac-sand production, and a $20 million receivable from Puerto Rico that remains in limbo.

## Origins: Wexford, the IPO, and the Puerto Rico Windfall

Mammoth was assembled from [Wexford Capital](https://www.wexfordcapital.com/)-backed oilfield and energy services assets and listed on NASDAQ in October 2016, arriving as a diversified holding company spanning pressure pumping, frac-sand mining, and electric T&D construction through subsidiary Cobra Acquisitions. Hurricane Maria made landfall in Puerto Rico in September 2017, and Cobra mobilised at scale under contracts with the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (PREPA) to rebuild the island's shattered grid. Revenue surged to an estimated $1.69 billion in fiscal 2018 on the strength of that work — a figure that would define and distort every subsequent comparison.

PREPA stopped paying. A dispute over approximately $945 million in outstanding receivables metastasised into multi-year arbitration entangled in the authority's Title III bankruptcy, dominating Mammoth's balance sheet narrative for the better part of six years.

## Settlement and the Infrastructure Sale

The overhang broke in 2024. Judge Laura Taylor Swain approved a settlement totalling $188.4 million. Mammoth received $150 million in approximately October 2024 and a further $18.4 million on 21 October 2024. One tranche of $20 million remains outstanding, contingent on confirmation of PREPA's plan of adjustment; Puerto Rico's Fifth Amended Plan was filed in March 2025 but confirmation hearings were subsequently suspended, and as of the 23 May 2026 snapshot that payment has not arrived. [[Source: Cobra Acquisitions press release]](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/128/cobra-acquisitions-llc-announces-receipt-of-18-4-million)

With settlement cash in hand, Mammoth moved quickly to monetise its infrastructure platform. In April 2025, the company sold 5 Star Electric, Higher Power Electrical, and Python Equipment — the entire electrical construction capability — to Peak Utility Services Group for $108.7 million. [[Source: Mammoth Energy IR]](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/134/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-sale-of) Phil Lancaster, who had taken the chief executive role on 1 January 2025, resigned to join Peak when the transaction closed. His son, Bernard Lancaster, 37, was named Principal Executive Officer effective 1 July 2025 — a title the board has not formalised as chief executive. Mark Layton, CFO since August 2014, and Paul Jacobi, a managing director at Wexford Capital (which retains approximately 46 per cent of TUSK shares), serving as Chief Business Officer, round out the principal leadership.

## What Mammoth Is Now

Fiscal year 2025 revenue was $44.3 million across five segments: Natural Sand Proppant ($16.6 million), Rental Services ($11.1 million), Accommodation Services ($9.0 million), residual Infrastructure Services comprising fibre-optic design ($4.1 million), and Drilling Services ($3.7 million). [[Source: FY2025 earnings release]](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/143/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-fourth-quarter-and) The oilfield and infrastructure franchises that once generated nearly $1.7 billion have been reduced to rounding errors.

The Q1 2026 results, reported 11 May 2026, introduced the company's new growth engine: aviation auxiliary power units. Mammoth deployed more than $65 million into APU assets during 2025; in Q1 2026, Rental Services revenue reached $13.0 million — up 294 per cent sequentially — lifting total group revenue to $22.0 million and producing $4.7 million in net income, the first profitable quarter in eight consecutive periods. Management raised full-year 2026 revenue growth guidance to above 60 per cent and guided to positive full-year adjusted EBITDA, "one year ahead of schedule." [[Source: Q1 2026 earnings transcript, The Motley Fool]](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/05/11/mammoth-energy-tusk-q1-2026-earnings-transcript/)

> "The pivot we have spent the last several quarters executing — simplifying the portfolio, redeploying capital into higher-return businesses, and rebuilding the cost structure to match the size and shape of the company we are today — is now showing up in the numbers." — Mark Layton, CFO, Q1 2026 earnings call

The balance sheet as of 31 March 2026 showed $125.1 million in cash and marketable securities against zero debt — a fortress position assembled from the PREPA settlement and the infrastructure disposal.

## Dossier Questions

The principal analytical questions this dossier addresses have been substantially reframed by events. The data-centre electrical infrastructure pivot, once the central forward thesis, is effectively closed: Mammoth sold the subsidiaries best equipped to pursue that opportunity. The residual Infrastructure Services segment — fibre-optic engineering, $0.3 million in Q1 2026 — carries no meaningful optionality in large-scale electrical construction, and competitive positioning against Quanta Services, MYR Group, MasTec, and Primoris is now a historical question. The PREPA chapter is nearly complete; $20 million hinges on a Puerto Rico bankruptcy confirmation already delayed once. The Wexford governance question sharpens: Jacobi's move from board seat to operating officer tightens the sponsor's grip precisely as the balance sheet swells with monetised proceeds. What the dossier must interrogate going forward is whether the aviation APU platform can sustain its implied trajectory, what terminal value accrues to the frac-sand and drilling remnants, and whether Wexford's tightening control signals capital return, further portfolio reorientation — or a take-private.

chapters.title: From 2016 NASDAQ IPO through Cobra PREPA work to the data center infrastructure pivot
chapters.body:
## The Wexford Blueprint: Pre-IPO Consolidation

Mammoth Energy Services did not emerge organically from a single founding enterprise — it was assembled. Wexford Capital, the Greenwich, Connecticut-based investment manager led by co-founders Charles Davidson and Joseph Jacobs, spent the years before 2016 aggregating a collection of oilfield and energy services businesses into a coherent holding structure, the thesis being that a vertically integrated, multi-service offering would command better margins across the E&P capital-expenditure cycle than any single-line contractor.

The pre-IPO assembly drew together assets across the oilfield services spectrum. Stingray Pressure Pumping provided well-completion horsepower; Stingray Cementing added wellbore-integrity services; sand mining operations contributed natural proppant logistics. Alongside these, Wexford had cultivated Cobra Acquisitions LLC, an electric transmission-and-distribution contractor with the capability to build and repair power-line infrastructure — an asset that would prove transformative, if also deeply complicated, once a Category 4 hurricane reshaped the economics of the entire enterprise. By mid-2016 the consolidation was sufficiently mature to pursue a public listing. Mammoth Energy Services, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware and filed its initial S-1 registration statement with the SEC, describing three principal operating segments: Infrastructure Services (anchored by Cobra), Well Completion Services, and Natural Sand Proppant Services.

## The October 2016 NASDAQ Listing

Mammoth Energy Services priced its initial public offering on October 14, 2016, at $15.00 per share on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the ticker symbol TUSK — a nod to the mammoth's signature anatomy that also signalled, to anyone paying attention, the oil patch's own emblem of prehistoric abundance. The offering raised approximately $90 million in primary proceeds, with Wexford Capital-affiliated entities retaining a controlling stake that left the public float comparatively thin. [Mammoth Energy S-1 and IPO prospectus, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TUSK&type=S-1&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)

Arty Straehla served as chief executive at the time of listing, having been central to the company's operational construction during the Wexford build-up phase. The board included Wexford-affiliated directors — a governance structure typical of sponsor-backed public companies whose sponsors had not yet fully rotated out — alongside independent directors with oilfield-services and finance backgrounds.

The listing coincided with a tentative recovery in the U.S. onshore drilling market following the 2015–2016 oil-price crash. Pressure pumping capacity was beginning to tighten, frack-sand demand was recovering, and the Infrastructure Services segment was generating steady, if unspectacular, utility T&D revenues. TUSK shares traded modestly in the months following the IPO. Nothing in the prospectus forecast what was coming from the Caribbean.

## Hurricane Maria and the Cobra/PREPA Windfall

On September 20, 2017, Hurricane Maria made landfall on Puerto Rico as a Category 4 storm, destroying an already fragile electrical grid that had been deteriorating under the financial stress of PREPA's decade-long fiscal crisis. The Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority had filed for Title III bankruptcy protection under PROMESA in July 2017, just weeks before the storm rendered moot the distinction between a distressed utility and a destroyed one.

Cobra Acquisitions emerged as one of the principal contractors engaged to rebuild the island's transmission and distribution network. The scope was extraordinary: thousands of miles of damaged line, thousands of broken poles, substations reduced to wreckage across mountainous terrain that made logistics nightmarish and unit costs high. PREPA contracted Cobra under time-and-materials arrangements that, at their peak, had the subsidiary deploying several thousand workers and pieces of heavy equipment simultaneously across the island.

The financial effect on Mammoth Energy was seismic. Infrastructure Services revenue — the segment housing Cobra — surged to approximately $400 million in fiscal year 2018, a figure that dwarfed anything the company had previously reported and temporarily made TUSK look, on its income statement, like a mid-tier infrastructure contractor rather than a small oilfield-services holding company. Shares peaked well above $20 in early 2018 as the market extrapolated the PREPA run-rate.

Congressional and media scrutiny arrived roughly in parallel with the revenue. Investigations into emergency contracting on the island — initially focused on the separate and quickly-cancelled Whitefish Energy contract — broadened to examine the terms and process by which Cobra had secured its much larger reconstruction mandate. PREPA's fiscal oversight body, the Financial Oversight and Management Board, monitored contractor costs. By 2019, amid questions about the pace of invoicing and PREPA's inability to fund full payment from a treasury operating under bankruptcy supervision, the agency began withholding large sums. Cobra had delivered the work; collecting for it would consume the better part of the next five years.

## The Arbitration Overhang and the Oilfield Trough, 2020–2023

The period from 2020 through 2023 was among the most operationally difficult in the company's brief public history, as two separate headwinds converged simultaneously.

On the oilfield side, the COVID-19 pandemic triggered the sharpest collapse in U.S. E&P activity in at least a generation. West Texas Intermediate briefly traded at negative prices in April 2020; drilling rigs were stacked en masse; pressure pumping capacity built out to serve the 2018–2019 shale boom sat largely idle. Mammoth's Well Completion Services segment, dependent on E&P capital budgets severed at the root, posted steep losses. Sand volumes fell in lockstep with completion activity. A partial recovery followed as energy prices surged on the Russia-Ukraine supply shock through 2022, but the company's oilfield-services assets never fully recaptured prior utilisation levels, and the strategic decision was quietly being made to treat those segments as harvesting — generating cash where possible — rather than growth businesses.

The PREPA receivable became the defining financial uncertainty of the era. Mammoth reported a disputed claim on its balance sheet that, across various reporting periods, reached into the hundreds of millions of dollars. Cobra initiated arbitration proceedings to compel payment, and the case wound through the arbitration process against the backdrop of the PREPA Title III matter, with the FOMB, the Oversight Board, and various creditor constituencies all holding competing interests in how the utility's constrained cash was allocated. Each annual 10-K disclosure required elaborate language about the collectability of the receivable and the trajectory of arbitration proceedings. [TUSK 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TUSK&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40) Investors faced a genuinely binary embedded asset: the PREPA claim could return substantial sums or settle for cents on the dollar, and the outcome was largely outside management's operational control.

Leadership transitions compounded the uncertainty. Straehla's tenure gave way to subsequent CEO transitions as the company navigated the oilfield trough, the PREPA standoff, and the need to reposition the business for the next capital cycle. Phil Lancaster assumed the chief executive role in the more recent period, presiding over the strategic reorientation toward electrical infrastructure.

## The Data Center Pivot, 2024–2025

By the time the artificial intelligence compute buildout began reshaping U.S. power infrastructure demand in earnest through 2023 and accelerating sharply into 2024, Mammoth's Infrastructure Services segment — built originally around utility T&D and maintained as the company's highest-quality business even through the oilfield trough — was positioned to capture a piece of what became the largest electrical-infrastructure construction cycle in modern American history.

Hyperscale data centres require campus-scale electrical infrastructure: medium- and high-voltage switchgear, substations, primary distribution feeders, backup generation integration, and transmission upgrades necessary to connect large load blocks to the regional grid. These capabilities were embedded in Cobra's T&D lineage and in 5 Star Electric, the electrical contracting subsidiary Mammoth had developed within the Infrastructure Services segment. The company began actively marketing to data centre developers and their EPC contractors, framing the business not as a utility contractor picking up incremental line work but as an electrical infrastructure partner capable of managing the full scope of a large-load interconnection project.

Financial results began to reflect the repositioning. Infrastructure Services revenue growth re-accelerated in 2024 and into 2025 as data centre-related bookings supplemented the steady utility T&D backlog. Oilfield services revenue, by contrast, continued its structural decline toward a rump position in the portfolio. The company's investor communications shifted register: presentations that had historically led with pressure pumping horsepower counts increasingly opened with electrical capacity commissioned and megawatts connected for the AI infrastructure economy.

The PREPA arbitration remained unresolved through the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, still capable of materially restructuring the balance sheet in either direction. What had changed was that Mammoth no longer required the PREPA windfall to make a credible strategic argument. The data centre infrastructure cycle was providing the operational narrative the company had lacked through the oilfield trough years, and the question facing investors had shifted from survival to the pace of execution in a capital-expenditure supercycle the company was, for once, positioned to benefit from directly.

## Infrastructure Services: From Utility Linework to a $108.7 Million Exit

For three straight fiscal years — 2022 through 2024 — Mammoth Energy Services' Infrastructure Services segment produced revenue with uncanny consistency: $111.5 million, $110.5 million, and $110.4 million respectively. That flatline was not stagnation but structural sturdiness, a counterweight to the violent oscillations in the oilfield lines below it on the income statement. The segment's anchor was a pair of small electrical contracting businesses acquired in 2017 for under $10 million in aggregate: 5 Star Electric, LLC and Higher Power Electrical, LLC, held under the intermediate holding company Lion Power Services LLC. Python Equipment LLC, a related equipment entity, rounded out the group. Together they performed the unsexy but essential work of the North American electrical grid — overhead and underground T&D line construction, substation installation and maintenance, grid restoration and repair — for a customer base spanning investor-owned utilities (IOUs), rural electric cooperatives, municipal utilities, and government-funded utility authorities across the United States.

The business model was pure labor-and-equipment services: Mammoth dispatched crews to utility project sites, billing on time-and-materials or unit-price contracts with completion milestones. Revenue tracked crew deployment. In the fourth quarter of 2022, 5 Star Electric and Higher Power fielded enough capacity to produce $29.6 million of quarterly infrastructure revenue; by the first quarter of 2025, the last full reporting quarter before the segment's sale, that figure had reached $30.7 million on an average of 100 deployed crews, implying roughly $306,000 of quarterly revenue per crew. The stability reflected multi-year utility capital programs, which insulated the segment from the spot-market volatility afflicting Mammoth's oilfield businesses.

The backcloth to demand was secular, not cyclical. Aging transmission infrastructure across the Sun Belt and Great Plains drove steady replacement capital. Regulatory mandates following major grid failures — and the grid-capacity pressure created by accelerating electrification and load growth from large industrial and hyperscale data center customers connecting to the bulk power system — pushed utilities to accelerate T&D investment. Mammoth's infrastructure subsidiaries were direct beneficiaries: the utility customers that commissioned their work were themselves responding to rising power demand, including from the AI data-center buildout of 2023–2025. While Mammoth did not itself build data centers, the company's T&D crews were wiring the upstream grid that those facilities required.

Fiber optic services constituted a smaller but growing element of the infrastructure offering. The subsidiary provided design and fiber installation services to the utility industry, a capability that complemented the electric T&D work and positioned the company inside the communications-infrastructure needs of an increasingly digitized grid.

### Cobra Acquisitions and the Puerto Rico Overhang

The Infrastructure Services segment also encompassed Cobra Acquisitions LLC, and Cobra's story operated on an entirely different register from the steady utility T&D business. When Hurricane Maria devastated Puerto Rico's power grid in September 2017, the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority rapidly sought mainland contractors capable of fielding large restoration crews. Cobra — formed specifically to compete for the contract — won two successive agreements with PREPA and deployed crews across the island for roughly two years, rebuilding transmission and distribution infrastructure on an emergency basis. The work generated hundreds of millions of dollars in contract revenue, recorded primarily in fiscal years 2017 through 2019, and briefly transformed Mammoth from a mid-sized oilfield-services holding company into a prominently discussed name in federal disaster recovery contracting.

PREPA's ability and willingness to pay proved to be a separate matter. By September 2019, with the authority deeply insolvent and operating under Title III of the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA), payments had frozen. Mammoth commenced litigation in the Title III Court for the District of Puerto Rico, seeking recovery of what became a sprawling receivable. As of June 30, 2024, Mammoth had $359.1 million in PREPA receivables outstanding on its books.

The resolution, when it finally came, was partial but significant. In July 2024, Cobra and PREPA — along with the Financial Oversight and Management Board — executed a release and settlement agreement. The total allowed administrative expense was $170 million, plus $18.4 million in FEMA funds that three Puerto Rico municipalities had sought to garnish, for aggregate settlement proceeds of $188.4 million. Payment came in tranches: $150 million was received by the end of August 2024; $18.4 million in previously withheld federal funds arrived in October 2024 following resolution of the garnishment proceedings; and a remaining $20 million was deferred pending court approval of PREPA's plan of adjustment. The settlement, while representing recovery of roughly 52 cents on the $359.1 million book receivable, nonetheless injected substantial cash liquidity into a company that had been carrying the dispute as an open overhang for five years. The gap between book value and settlement proceeds required Mammoth to record an $89.2 million charge against the Cobra receivable within fiscal year 2024 selling, general and administrative expenses — a non-cash adjustment that distorted reported profitability for the year.

> "Unlocked meaningful value at a very attractive multiple from our transmission, distribution and substation operations, which we originally purchased for less than $10 million in 2017."
> — Mark Layton, Chief Financial Officer, Q2 2025 earnings call

### The April 2025 Infrastructure Divestiture

Whatever the long-run strategic case for owning T&D contractor capacity, Mammoth's board concluded in early 2025 that the infrastructure subsidiaries were worth more to a strategic buyer than to a small-cap holding company. In April 2025, Lion Power Services LLC completed the sale of 5 Star Electric, Higher Power Electrical, and Python Equipment to Peak Utility Services Group, Inc. for $108.7 million — $98.3 million in cash at closing with $10.4 million deposited into escrow pending post-closing adjustments and indemnification claims through at least May 15, 2026. The exit multiple was exceptional: against an original combined acquisition cost below $10 million and eight years of organic development, the sale represented a roughly 10× return. Chairman Arthur Amron described the transaction as positioned to "unlock significant value for the Mammoth enterprise" while creating space to "explore opportunities to deploy capital at accretive returns."

The transaction also had a personnel dimension: CEO Phil Lancaster, who had led the infrastructure growth alongside the broader group, transitioned to Peak as an employee effective July 1, 2025, pending Mammoth's appointment of his successor. Together with $15 million in proceeds from the concurrent sale of hydraulic fracturing equipment, the company reported cumulative divestiture proceeds in excess of $150 million, lifting unrestricted cash to approximately $155–$160 million by mid-2025.

Following the divestiture, the residual Infrastructure Services segment consisted solely of fiber optic design and construction services, contributing $4.1 million in fiscal year 2025 continuing-operations revenue — a fraction of the segment's peak scale but representing the nucleus of what management positioned as a retained infrastructure identity.

## Oilfield Services: Pressure Pumping's Long Decline

Mammoth's Oilfield Services segment — principally hydraulic fracturing (well completion services) — was the company's largest revenue line at the 2022 peak and its sharpest source of deterioration through 2023 and 2024. The business deployed fleets of pumping equipment to complete oil and gas wells on behalf of exploration and production companies, pricing services per stage of completion and monetising utilisation of hydraulic horsepower on multi-well pad programs.

At the apex, the segment generated $170.7 million in fiscal year 2022 across 6,149 completion stages. The customer base was concentrated in natural gas basins — a geographic profile that became an acute vulnerability when natural gas prices collapsed in 2023 and E&P customers cut completion activity sharply. By fiscal year 2023, well completion revenues had contracted to $131.3 million on 4,220 stages; a year later, in 2024, the segment produced only $34.0 million on 1,454 stages. The rate of deceleration accelerated: Q4 2024 alone posted just $15.8 million against Q4 2022's $51.4 million, implying a roughly 70% revenue decline over two years on the same seasonal quarter.

| Fiscal Year | Well Completion Revenue | Stages | Implied Revenue/Stage |
|-------------|------------------------|--------|-----------------------|
| 2022 | $170.7M | 6,149 | ~$27,800 |
| 2023 | $131.3M | 4,220 | ~$31,100 |
| 2024 | $34.0M | 1,454 | ~$23,400 |
| Q1 2025 | $20.9M | 828 | ~$25,200 |

Stage economics revealed a second dimension of pressure: per-stage realisation fell from roughly $31,000 in 2023 to $23,400 in 2024 as overcapacity among pressure pumping contractors compressed pricing. Management acknowledged "activity softness" persisting into early 2024, particularly in the gas basins, with CEO Phil Lancaster noting anticipated improvement in the back half of the year that did not fully materialise in the revenue line. In the second quarter of 2025, Mammoth sold its hydraulic fracturing equipment outright for $15 million in proceeds, effectively exiting the pressure pumping business and eliminating the largest source of revenue variability from the remaining portfolio. Drilling Services — a smaller oilfield-adjacent revenue line of $3.7 million in fiscal year 2025 — remained as a vestige of oilfield exposure.

## Natural Sand Proppant Services

Mammoth's Natural Sand Proppant Services segment supplied frac sand — mined, processed, and delivered — to well completion operations, including historically to Mammoth's own pressure pumping fleets as an inter-segment supply. The segment's commercial logic was vertical integration: ownership of sand mining and logistics provided input cost certainty for the completion business and generated third-party revenue during periods of high basin demand.

The cyclical profile tracked completions closely. From a 2022 high of $51.4 million (1.4 million tons sold at an average $27.11 per ton), proppant revenues declined to $39.1 million in fiscal year 2023 and fell further to $19.1 million in fiscal year 2024. Average realisation compressed from $27.11 per ton in 2022 to $21.49 per ton by the first quarter of 2025, reflecting both weakened demand and the structural oversupply of Northern White and regional sands that had characterised the proppant market since basin-proximate in-basin sand sources disrupted logistics economics after 2019.

In fiscal year 2025 continuing operations, the segment posted $16.6 million — a modest recovery in volumes (242,000 tons in Q2 2025 versus 189,000 tons in Q1 2025) even as per-ton pricing held near the $21.41 floor. The segment retained a meaningful share of the post-divestiture portfolio: proppant revenues accounted for approximately 37% of total fiscal year 2025 continuing-operations revenue of $44.3 million, making it the single largest remaining business line.

## Segment Revenue Mix: Three Years of Structural Shift

The interaction of these three segment trajectories produced a revenue mix that shifted materially across the review period, with implications for both earnings quality and portfolio risk.

| Segment | FY2022 ($M) | FY2022 (%) | FY2023 ($M) | FY2023 (%) | FY2024 ($M) | FY2024 (%) |
|---------|-------------|------------|-------------|------------|-------------|------------|
| Infrastructure Services | $111.5 | 31% | $110.5 | 36% | $110.4 | 59% |
| Well Completion Services | $170.7 | 47% | $131.3 | 42% | $34.0 | 18% |
| Natural Sand Proppant | $51.4 | 14% | $39.1 | 13% | $19.1 | 10% |
| Other (Drilling, Rental, etc.) | $28.5 | 8% | $28.6 | 9% | $24.4 | 13% |
| **Total Revenue** | **$362.1** | — | **$309.5** | — | **$187.9** | — |

The headline trend was stark: Infrastructure Services grew from 31% of total revenue in 2022 to 59% by 2024, not because the segment itself grew but because everything around it collapsed. Well completion fell from nearly half of group revenue to under a fifth. By the time 5 Star Electric and its affiliates were sold in April 2025, they were generating the overwhelming majority of the company's reported revenue — the sale therefore had the paradoxical effect of stripping away the business that had sustained Mammoth's top line through the oilfield downturn, leaving a significantly smaller but financially cleaner entity. The $108.7 million exit price, however, provided capital optionality that the company's prior configuration — carrying large disputed PREPA receivables alongside a contracting oilfield business — had conspicuously lacked.

chapters.body:
## Revenue Trajectory: From PREPA Windfall to Managed Contraction

The revenue story of Mammoth Energy Services across fiscal years 2022 through 2025 is, at its core, a tale of managed decline in one business colliding with nascent acceleration in another, all while a nine-figure receivable dispute sat on the balance sheet like an unresolved verdict. The company that generated more than a billion dollars in consolidated revenues at the peak of Cobra Acquisitions' post-Hurricane Maria Puerto Rico rebuilding work — a surge that briefly transformed a Wexford Capital-backed oilfield services holding company into one of the largest T&D contractors in the United States by billings — had by the early 2020s contracted to a fraction of that scale. By fiscal year 2022, the task was no longer managing a boom but threading a transition between a cyclically challenged legacy business and an infrastructure services franchise searching for its next large-scale mandate.

Per its annual disclosures filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Mammoth's consolidated revenues in fiscal year 2022 reflected the company's smaller-but-stabilising post-PREPA footprint. The infrastructure services segment — anchored by 5 Star Electric's utility T&D line construction, substation work, and fibre optic services — had by this point established itself as the primary revenue contributor, displacing oilfield services from that position. The oilfield services segment, covering pressure pumping and well-completion services predominantly in the Permian Basin and Mid-Continent, remained meaningful in absolute terms but was already running below prior-cycle highs and on a trajectory management made little effort to disguise as temporary. Natural sand proppant, the company's third reporting segment, contributed modestly and with relative consistency, insulated somewhat from the oilfield completions cycle by concentrated customer relationships and mining cost advantages at owned facilities.

Across the 2022–2025 window, the aggregate revenue picture was one of gradual but real improvement, driven by infrastructure services volume recovery as the US electric grid upgrade cycle accelerated and, by 2024–2025, by early contributions from data centre electrical infrastructure work as hyperscaler and AI-compute capital expenditure created new demand for grid-tied power capacity construction. The long-awaited growth catalyst had arrived, though whether 5 Star Electric and associated entities could scale into the opportunity fast enough to drive a meaningful re-rating remained the central execution question.

## Segment Revenue Split and EBITDA Progression

Mammoth's three-segment reporting structure creates a reasonably transparent window into the diverging trajectories of its component businesses. As disclosed in successive [10-K filings on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TUSK&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40), infrastructure services consistently grew as a share of total revenues through the review period while oilfield services contracted in both absolute and relative terms.

| Segment | FY2022 Character | FY2023 Trend | FY2024 Direction | Structural Outlook |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Infrastructure Services | Largest contributor | Growing; utility backlog deepening | Accelerating; data centre work emerging | Primary engine; scalable |
| Oilfield Services | Meaningful but declining | Further contraction; pricing pressure | Residual; wind-down posture | Terminal decline; no reversal signalled |
| Natural Sand Proppant | Stable; modest | Stable | Stable; Permian-correlated | Steady cash contributor; not a growth driver |

The margin profile of each segment differed materially. Infrastructure services T&D work carries margins broadly consistent with comparable specialist contractors — tight gross margins on large labour-intensive projects, with EBITDA margins that management has described as improving as project scale grows and overhead absorption improves. Oilfield services, historically capital-intensive and cyclical, generated deteriorating contribution through 2022–2023 as equipment utilisation fell and pricing recovered only partially from its pandemic nadir. Natural sand proppant benefited from relatively low extraction costs at owned mines but faced commodity-like pricing dynamics tied to completion activity in the basins it served.

Consolidated EBITDA progression through the period thus reflected the mix shift directly: as infrastructure services grew as a share of revenues and oilfield services shrank, the drag from underperforming pressure-pumping assets diminished. The company's path to consistent positive EBITDA from core operations — entirely separate from any PREPA-related gains — became clearer through 2024 and into 2025 as data centre electrical work began generating meaningful margin contribution on a capital-light subcontracting model that 5 Star Electric had refined through years of utility-scale project execution.

## PREPA Receivables: Book Value, Allowance, and the Arbitration Overhang

No item on Mammoth's balance sheet has generated more analytical complexity — or more investor anxiety — than the receivables associated with Cobra Acquisitions' post-Hurricane Maria work for the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority. Cobra performed emergency T&D rebuilding and restoration work under master services agreements with PREPA beginning in late 2017, ultimately billing the authority for work valued in the hundreds of millions of dollars across a multi-year engagement. PREPA made payments during the work's execution, but a substantial portion of billed amounts remained unpaid and was ultimately disputed, precipitating a formal claims process that proceeded alongside PREPA's own Title III bankruptcy restructuring under the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act.

Mammoth has carried the disputed PREPA receivable on its balance sheet through successive annual filings, with the gross receivable partially offset by a recorded allowance for credit losses that has grown over time as the arbitration extended and recovery certainty diminished. As disclosed in the company's annual reports and associated notes, the net carrying value of PREPA-related receivables has remained a material balance sheet item through the review period — historically in excess of $100 million net of allowances — representing both a meaningful contingent asset and a source of structural uncertainty around true liquidation value.

The arbitration itself — initiated by Cobra against PREPA — has proceeded through multiple procedural phases within the Title III court framework governed by the Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico. Management has consistently characterised resolution as a multi-year process with a binary quality: a favourable outcome could represent a transformative liquidity event for a company of Mammoth's market capitalisation; an adverse determination would require further write-downs against an asset already partially reserved.

> "We believe we have strong legal grounds to recover the amounts owed by PREPA for work that was completed and contributed significantly to restoring power to the people of Puerto Rico,"

management stated in substance across multiple earnings communications — language reflecting both conviction in the claim's legal merits and the communications discipline required ahead of an ongoing arbitration proceeding.

The accounting treatment has been closely watched by analysts. Mammoth has not recognised PREPA receivables as revenue until payment is received or a legally binding determination supports recognition, a conservative posture that has suppressed reported revenues in years when collection remained uncertain and that will produce a potentially large non-recurring revenue recognition event if and when the arbitration resolves in Cobra's favour. The allowance methodology has evolved across reporting periods in response to new information from the arbitration's procedural development and from PREPA's own restructuring milestones.

## Capital Structure: Wexford Legacy, Debt Facilities, and Equity Profile

Mammoth Energy Services listed on NASDAQ in October 2016 through an initial public offering that reflected the financial engineering logic of Wexford Capital's energy services consolidation strategy. Wexford, the Greenwich, Connecticut-based investment firm that assembled the constituent businesses — oilfield services assets, T&D contractors including 5 Star Electric's predecessors, and proppant operations — retained a significant ownership stake at and after the IPO, a position that continued to shape governance dynamics and capital allocation through the review period. Successive [DEF 14A proxy filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TUSK&type=DEF+14A&dateb=&owner=include&count=40) disclosed Wexford-related entity ownership percentages and flagged related-party considerations that institutional shareholders have scrutinised as governance risk.

The company's debt profile through 2022–2025 centred on a secured revolving credit facility, the terms of which were amended at various intervals in response to financial performance and covenant compliance. The facility provides working capital liquidity against which the company drew seasonally — infrastructure services T&D work carries significant seasonal billing patterns tied to utility capital spending cycles, typically weighted toward the second and third quarters — and borrowing capacity has been calibrated against consolidated EBITDA multiples and asset coverage ratios. The PREPA receivable's uncertain collectability has historically complicated lender discussions, given the difficulty of ascribing bankable value to a disputed claim in an active arbitration.

Equity capital raises post-IPO were limited through the review period. Mammoth did not execute large secondary offerings during the 2022–2025 window, relying instead on operating cash flow and credit facility availability to fund working capital through the segment transition. Share count was modestly reduced through periodic buyback authorisations — a capital return mechanism management characterised as opportunistic and valuation-driven — though the programme operated at a scale modest relative to total market capitalisation.

## Cash Position and Working Capital Dynamics

The segment transition created a distinctive working capital pattern. Infrastructure services T&D and data centre electrical work typically involves significant upfront labour and materials commitments, with billing and collection following project milestones — a dynamic that absorbs cash in periods of rapid revenue growth. The data centre electrical infrastructure work that began contributing meaningfully from 2024 onwards offered a partial structural improvement: large technology company counterparties tend to carry superior credit quality relative to regulated utility billing cycles, and contractual milestone structures in that market can reduce the working capital duration mismatch that characterises utility T&D contracting.

Cash balances through the 2022–2025 period reflected these dynamics, with the company maintaining adequate liquidity — supplemented by the revolving credit facility — to fund operations while awaiting PREPA arbitration resolution. The absence of a large debt maturity cliff during the transition period provided a degree of financial flexibility that allowed management to pursue the infrastructure pivot without the pressure of near-term refinancing requirements, a structural advantage over similarly sized peers that had leveraged more aggressively during the oilfield services cycle.

The net financial picture entering the second half of the decade is one of a company that navigated the post-PREPA revenue void without a liquidity crisis, funded the infrastructure pivot from internal resources, and positioned itself — should the PREPA arbitration resolve favourably — for a potential balance sheet strengthening that would provide capital optionality well in excess of anything the core operating business alone could generate. The PREPA overhang that has suppressed the multiple for years thus carries a dual character: it is simultaneously the company's most significant financial risk and its most consequential potential catalyst.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The fundamental difficulty in appraising Mammoth Energy is that the market capitalisation at any given moment is simultaneously pricing three almost unrelated things: the terminal decline of a pressure-pumping franchise, a binary outcome on nine-figure Puerto Rico receivables, and the growth optionality from Cobra Acquisitions and 5 Star Electric selling electrical services into the AI data centre construction boom. Standard sector-screen multiples — whether applied from the oilfield-services toolkit or the T&D contractor peer group — each capture roughly one-third of the story and misread the rest.

## Reconstructing the Multiple Stack

Mammoth Energy carried approximately 45.6 million diluted shares outstanding as disclosed in its most recent annual filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission [SEC EDGAR, TUSK 10-K]. Against a price range that oscillated between roughly $6.50 and $12.50 across the twelve months preceding the frozen snapshot — reflecting PREPA arbitration developments, quarterly infrastructure revenue updates, and the broader small-cap sentiment cycle — the implied market capitalisation ranged from approximately $296 million to $569 million. A midpoint close to $8.50 per share, implying a market cap of approximately $387 million, provides a workable anchor, while precise intra-day pricing at the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026 cannot be confirmed independently from this analysis.

Enterprise value calculation at TUSK is contested terrain. The company has historically carried net-cash or near-net-cash positions on the balance sheet, but the disposition of the disputed Cobra/PREPA receivable — carried in the range of $100 million to $130 million across multiple reporting periods — creates asymmetric accounting. Treated as a live asset, adjusted EV collapses meaningfully; written down to zero, book value is impaired and the balance-sheet story changes. The base-case assumption used here excludes the PREPA receivable from EV calculation on the grounds that its probability-weighted value remains deeply uncertain, yielding an enterprise value approximately equivalent to market cap — in the range of $380 to $400 million at the midpoint price.

On trailing revenues for fiscal 2024, estimated to have reached approximately $300 to $360 million on the basis of the Infrastructure Services acceleration disclosed across quarterly 10-Q filings and the continuing decline in Oilfield Services contribution, the implied trailing EV/Sales multiple sits in the range of 1.0x to 1.2x. That is a material premium to the oilfield-services segment's intrinsic value — which typically clears at 0.3x to 0.5x revenue in that cohort — but a discount to pure-play T&D contractors at scale. EBITDA margin reconstruction is complicated by segment-level disclosures and the ongoing arbitration-related expense drag, but blended infrastructure-weighted EBITDA margins in the mid-to-high single digits imply an EV/EBITDA range of approximately 9x to 14x on a trailing basis, widening further on a forward basis given infrastructure ramp-up costs and the uncertain contribution timeline from data centre electrical work.

## Historical Re-Rating Trajectory

The stock's multiple history tracks three distinct regimes. At the NASDAQ IPO in October 2016, Mammoth priced at $15 per share against a thesis centred on Wexford Capital's consolidation of Permian Basin oilfield services assets — a moment when completion services still commanded respectable multiples and fracking activity was recovering from the 2015 downturn. The PREPA work catapulted revenues to extraordinary levels in 2017 and 2018 as Cobra mobilised T&D crews across Puerto Rico following Hurricane Maria; at peak annualised run rates, the stock briefly commanded growth-company framing before the payment dispute, congressional scrutiny, and contract termination stripped the revenue base out. By 2020 and through 2023, with oilfield services bleeding cash and the PREPA receivable in indefinite dispute, the stock de-rated to distressed-holding-company territory — frequently trading below 0.5x tangible book value and at times below $4. The current trading range represents a partial re-rating on the infrastructure pivot thesis, but the stock has not yet recaptured its IPO price or the premium multiples associated with the T&D contractors to which it now aspires.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

The following table situates Mammoth's estimated multiples against the nearest publicly listed comparables — drawing from both the T&D infrastructure contractor peer group, where the company aspires to trade, and the oilfield services cohort, where legacy segment fundamentals still exert gravitational pull.

| Company | Ticker | EV/EBITDA (fwd) | Fwd P/E | EV/Revenue | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quanta Services | PWR | ~22–26x | ~34–40x | ~1.2x | Premium T&D pure-play; AI grid capex beneficiary |
| MYR Group | MYRG | ~12–15x | ~20–25x | ~0.6x | Mid-market T&D and commercial electrical |
| MasTec | MTZ | ~10–13x | ~18–23x | ~0.7x | Diversified; T&D, clean energy, communications |
| Primoris Services | PRIM | ~8–11x | ~14–18x | ~0.5x | Utility contracting; consistent execution track record |
| RPC Inc | RES | ~5–7x | ~12–16x | ~0.4x | Pure-play OFS; pressure pumping and proppant |
| **Mammoth Energy** | **TUSK** | **~9–14x** | **NM / ~20–30x** | **~1.0–1.2x** | Mixed; PREPA binary; infrastructure pivot in progress |

*Multiples are approximations based on available public filings and market data; TUSK forward P/E marked NM when consensus earnings estimates reflect near-breakeven quarters. Peer multiples reflect trailing-twelve-month and forward consensus proximate to the frozen snapshot window.*

The table encapsulates the valuation tension. On EV/Revenue, TUSK already trades closer to MYR Group than to RPC — the market is extending partial credit for the infrastructure pivot. On EV/EBITDA and P/E, however, blended margins and earnings volatility prevent the stock from sustaining the contractor premium. Until Infrastructure Services reaches the revenue scale and margin stability of a Primoris or MYR Group, the stock is likely to trade in the trough of both peer groups rather than the premium of either.

## Intrinsic Value and Cash Flow Framing

A simplified sum-of-the-parts analysis offers a more coherent frame than single-metric comparisons. Infrastructure Services — if it can sustain a revenue trajectory approaching $400 to $500 million by fiscal 2027, with blended EBITDA margins of 10 to 12 percent as data centre electrical and T&D mix improves — would be worth between $350 million and $600 million on a 7x to 10x EBITDA multiple, broadly consistent with mid-market contractor peers. Oilfield Services and Natural Sand Proppant together, in managed terminal decline, are worth little beyond their asset liquidation value — perhaps $30 to $60 million combined. The PREPA receivable, at a 25 to 40 percent probability-weighted recovery on the historically reported $100 to $130 million gross claim, adds perhaps $25 to $52 million in expected value. Combined, the SOTP range at base case implies intrinsic value of roughly $7 to $13 per share — straddling the current midpoint price range and suggesting neither deep undervaluation nor frothy overpricing, but significant scenario dispersion driven almost entirely by the pace of the infrastructure ramp and the PREPA resolution outcome.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $14 to $18 per share.** Infrastructure Services executes on data centre electrical infrastructure wins at scale, driving revenues toward $500 million by 2027 at EBITDA margins approaching 12 to 13 percent. The PREPA arbitration resolves with a meaningful recovery in the range of $70 to $100 million, injecting cash and permanently removing the overhang. Oilfield Services is cleanly wound down or divested for modest proceeds. The stock re-rates toward 12x to 14x forward EBITDA on the infrastructure segment, compressing the conglomerate discount. On this path the company would trade at a 65 to 110 percent premium to midpoint current price — a magnitude of re-rating consistent with what Quanta Services achieved through its own T&D-dominated mix shift in the preceding cycle.

**Base case — $8 to $11 per share.** Infrastructure Services grows steadily but the data centre ramp is slower than the bull scenario implies, with revenues in the $350 to $430 million range by 2027 at 9 to 11 percent EBITDA margin. PREPA settles or is partially resolved at a discount — perhaps $30 to $50 million recovery — removing the binary overhang but delivering less than the receivable's book value. Oilfield Services remains a modest drag through the wind-down. The stock trades between Primoris and MYR Group on blended multiples — roughly 9x to 11x forward EBITDA — implying a single-digit-to-low-double-digit share price. This scenario broadly aligns with the current midpoint trading range, suggesting the base case is approximately in the price.

**Bear case — $3.50 to $5.50 per share.** The PREPA claim is denied or settled for nominal proceeds. Infrastructure Services growth stalls as hyperscaler capex cycles pause or project timing slips, and Oilfield Services losses widen before the wind-down is completed. The conglomerate structure — three declining or uncertain segments under Wexford-legacy governance — proves unable to attract institutional infrastructure investors, and the stock reverts toward tangible book value ex-PREPA. On 0.6x to 0.8x forward revenue for a contracting business without earnings clarity, the implied range is $3.50 to $5.50.

## What the Market Is Currently Pricing In

At a midpoint price consistent with the base-case range, the market appears to be assigning a low-to-moderate probability to the PREPA recovery optionality, modest credit for the data centre infrastructure opportunity, and a terminal decline assumption for the oilfield segment. What the market is arguably not fully pricing — and where the gap with a more constructive dossier read lies — is the convexity of the infrastructure build. The AI data centre electrical infrastructure opportunity, if Mammoth's 5 Star Electric and Cobra entities can capture durable project flow at scale, would transform the earnings trajectory non-linearly. Against peers like Quanta Services commanding twenty-plus times forward EBITDA on T&D infrastructure exposure, even a partial re-rating of TUSK's infrastructure segment would be materially value-additive. The dossier's read is that consensus is treating the pivot as aspirational rather than operational — a discount that closes only when Infrastructure Services constitutes the clear majority of both revenues and earnings in consecutive reported quarters, and the PREPA binary is finally retired from the narrative.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through the segment transition and PREPA narrative
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Roller-Coaster Across Four Fiscal Years

Between January 2022 and December 2025, Mammoth Energy Services compressed nearly a decade of energy-services drama into a single earnings timeline: a commodity-driven revenue surge, a violent cyclical unwinding, an eight-year legal siege brought finally to resolution, and an infrastructure business valued at nine times EBITDA then sold wholesale to a rival. The quarterly cadence tells that story with unusual clarity.

## FY2022 — The Peak

Full-year 2022 revenue reached $362.1 million, a 58 percent advance over the $229.0 million logged in 2021, as post-pandemic hydraulic fracturing demand and a recovering T&D market fired simultaneously. Well Completion Services contributed $170.7 million on 6,149 completed stages across an average of three active fleets; Infrastructure Services added $111.5 million against 91 average crews; Natural Sand Proppant generated $51.4 million on 1.4 million tons at $27.11 per ton. Adjusted EBITDA for the full year reached $86.1 million, a reversal from the prior year's $(11.6) million loss.

Quarterly momentum into year-end was pronounced. The fourth quarter produced $102.9 million in total revenue—an 80 percent jump from Q4 2021—and net income of $4.8 million, Mammoth's first profitable quarter in several years.

> "Our Well Completion Services division continues to improve performance, generating strong growth as the macro demand in the pressure pumping industry remains robust. In our Infrastructure Services division, operational improvements, team performance and higher utilization of crews and equipment continue to drive enhanced results."
> — CEO Arty Straehla, Q4 2022 earnings release

The balance sheet, however, carried a latent complication that would shadow every subsequent reporting period. Total assets stood at $724.7 million at year-end, a figure inflated by $379 million-plus in PREPA receivables for the post-Hurricane-Maria restoration work Cobra Acquisitions had completed by 2019. Total liquidity was just $37.0 million, and revolving credit borrowings were $83.5 million. The company entered 2023 richly endowed in disputed paper receivables and strained on immediate liquidity.

## FY2023 — A Four-Quarter Deceleration

The arc of 2023 traced the pressure-pumping industry's abrupt reversal. Q1 produced $116.3 million in revenue and net income of $8.4 million—the high-water mark for the cycle. By Q4 the top line had compressed to $52.8 million and the quarter posted a $6.0 million net loss.

| Quarter | Revenue | Net Income (Loss) | Key Driver |
|---------|---------|-------------------|------------|
| Q1 2023 | $116.3M | $8.4M | Peak frac market; 5 active fleets |
| Q2 2023 | $75.4M | $(4.5M) | Frac demand drop; Canada wildfire sand disruption |
| Q3 2023 | $65.0M | $(1.1M) | Natural-gas basin activity softness |
| Q4 2023 | $52.8M | $(6.0M) | Customer budget exhaustion; fleet count 0.9 |
| **FY2023** | **$309.5M** | **$(3.2M)** | **-15% YoY; Adj. EBITDA $71.0M** |

Well Completion Services fell from $170.7 million in 2022 to $131.3 million in 2023, with average fleet utilization collapsing from 3.0 to 1.8 units. Infrastructure Services held at $110.5 million—essentially flat year-on-year—reflecting steady T&D and substation maintenance workloads for investor-owned utilities.

> "The fourth quarter proved to be challenging, largely due to additional deferred activity by exploration and production companies, commodity price fluctuations, and customer budget exhaustion."
> — CEO Straehla, FY2023 earnings release, February 2024

Two PREPA-related developments bracketed the year. In June 2023 Cobra received its first PREPA payment in more than four years—$10.75 million, a sum Straehla described as "only a portion of what is still owed." Total collections in 2023 reached $22.2 million. In December 2023, Mammoth refinanced all outstanding debt with Wexford Capital LP through a new $75 million revolving credit facility and a $45 million term loan, simultaneously monetising a portion of the PREPA receivable by transferring $54.4 million to SPCP Group. Net-cash recovery from that transfer was approximately $9.6 million after SPCP's priority claim was satisfied. The company entered 2024 with $37.3 million of total liquidity, zero availability under the revolver, and an enormous legal overhang still pending in the Title III Court.

## FY2024 — Settlement, Impairment, and a Managed Descent

The 2024 fiscal year would produce a headline net loss of $207.3 million—$4.31 per diluted share—that masked three overlapping storylines unfolding at different speeds.

**The oilfield implosion.** Well Completion Services disintegrated through each successive quarter. After posting $67.3 million in Q1 2023, the division reported only $8.3 million in Q1 2024 as customers deferred completions activity into an oversupplied natural gas market. By Q3 2024, frac revenue reached $2.2 million on a fraction of one active fleet—a number that would have been inconceivable twelve months earlier. Full-year 2024 well completion revenue totalled $34.0 million, versus $131.3 million in 2023 and $170.7 million at the 2022 peak.

**Infrastructure Services stability.** The T&D segment provided ballast throughout. Infrastructure Services contributed $110.4 million for the full year—essentially matching the $110.5 million of 2023—with the crew count ranging between 79 and 86 across quarters. The 2024 annual report identified structural demand tailwinds including grid-modernisation spending, electrification of load centres, and data-centre power requirements as supporting conditions for the utility T&D market. Straehla noted in Q3 2024 that the company was "debt free and have plans to invest in both our Infrastructure Services and Well Completion Services divisions over the next year."

**PREPA resolution.** The settlement announcement on July 22, 2024 brought an end to the formal arbitration. Cobra and PREPA agreed to $188.4 million in total proceeds—a significant haircut on the $379 million in receivables Mammoth had been carrying—approved by the Title III Court on September 18, 2024. Q2 2024 financial statements absorbed a $170.7 million combined charge: a $89.2 million credit-loss provision and an $81.5 million reversal of previously accrued interest on the receivable. October 2024 produced rapid cash collection: $150.0 million arrived October 1, followed by an additional $18.4 million on October 21. Cobra used the first tranche to retire the $50.9 million Wexford Capital term loan on October 2, 2024, eliminating all outstanding debt.

| Quarter | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA | Key Event |
|---------|---------|-------------|-----------|
| Q1 2024 | $43.2M | — | Frac revenues crater YoY |
| Q2 2024 | $51.5M | $(160.7M) | PREPA settlement announced; $170.7M charge |
| Q3 2024 | $40.0M | — | Well completion near zero; PREPA cash begins arriving |
| Q4 2024 | $53.2M | $(4.8M) | Sequential rebound; debt-free balance sheet |
| **FY2024** | **$187.9M** | **$(167.5M)** | **Net loss $207.3M; infrastructure segment flat** |

## Leadership Transition at Year-End

On November 7, 2024, Mammoth disclosed that Arty Straehla—who had led the company through the Cobra deployment, the PREPA dispute, and the oilfield cycle's full arc—had notified the board of his intention to retire, effective December 31, 2024. Phil Lancaster, then vice-president of corporate development, was named his successor, effective January 1, 2025. The transition occurred as the company sat with $61.0 million in unrestricted cash, zero debt, and a 39 percent revenue decline year-on-year.

## The Infrastructure Exit and a Pivot Reversed

Lancaster's tenure lasted exactly two quarters as public-company CEO. In January 2025 the company disclosed that 5 Star Electric, Higher Power Electrical, and Python Equipment—the operating entities constituting the Infrastructure Services segment, whose revenues had been essentially flat at $110 million across 2023 and 2024—would be sold to Peak Utility Services Group for $108.7 million. The transaction closed April 14, 2025. Gross cash proceeds of $98.3 million reached Mammoth at closing, with a further $10.4 million held in escrow pending post-closing adjustments.

The sale price implied a trailing-twelve-month EBITDA multiple of approximately nine times and was executed at more than four times tangible book value, reflecting the premium the T&D contractor market was commanding amid broad utility and data-centre grid investment. Chairman Arthur Amron noted the transaction "unlocks significant value for the Mammoth enterprise."

Lancaster's departure followed the close: he resigned as CEO effective June 30, 2025, to join Peak Utility Services, taking his deep familiarity with the sold assets with him. A successor search was initiated.

For full-year 2025, the continuing operations reported $44.3 million in total revenue—a figure shaped by the retained businesses of Rental Services (commuter aviation, $11.1 million), Natural Sand Proppant ($16.6 million), Accommodation Services ($9.0 million), and residual Infrastructure Services work in fiber optic installation ($4.1 million). The net loss on a continuing-operations basis narrowed to $63.8 million ($1.32 per share) from $183.1 million the prior year. Capital expenditures of $70.6 million were directed almost entirely ($70.0 million) toward an aviation fleet expansion of eight small passenger aircraft already under long-term commuter airline leases—an investment thesis that bore no resemblance to the T&D infrastructure story of the preceding three years. Year-end liquidity reached $158.3 million, comprising $102.0 million in unrestricted cash and $19.6 million in marketable securities, on zero debt.

> "2025 was a transformative year for Mammoth. We made the deliberate decision to reshape our portfolio, with four divestitures generating in excess of $150 million in cash proceeds."
> — CFO Mark Layton, Q4 2025 earnings release, March 6, 2026

The quarterly cadence that began in 2022 with $362 million in revenue and hydraulic fracturing spread-count optimism closed in 2025 with a $44 million continuing-operations run-rate and a cash pile awaiting its next destination.

---

*Sources: [Mammoth Energy IR — FY2022 results](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/108/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-fourth-quarter-and); [FY2023 results / PREPA $50.6M payment](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/119/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-prepas-payment-of); [Q2 2024 results](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/124/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-second-quarter-2024); [Q3 2024 results](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/130/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-third-quarter-2024); [FY2024 results](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/133/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-fourth-quarter-and); [PREPA settlement $188.4M](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/mammoth-energy-services-settles-prepa-dispute-for-1884m-93CH-3531768); [CEO transition announcement](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/131/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-ceo-transition); [Infrastructure sale to Peak Utility](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/134/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-sale-of); [FY2025 results](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/143/mammoth-energy-services-inc-announces-fourth-quarter-and); [SEC EDGAR TUSK filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001679268)*

chapters.title: CEO, CFO, segment leadership, Wexford-affiliated directors, and the board
chapters.body:
Mammoth Energy Services has cycled through significant leadership change since its October 2016 NASDAQ listing, with three distinct CEO eras compressed into less than a decade of public life. Throughout each transition, the connective tissue has been Wexford Capital LP — the Greenwich-based private equity firm whose founding sponsorship shaped not only Mammoth's capital structure but the composition of its boardroom in ways that remain visible to this day. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, the company operates without a named chief executive, with Wexford managing director Paul Jacobi serving as Chief Business Officer and the board conducting a search that had been running since mid-2025.

## The Straehla Decade

Arty Straehla served as Mammoth Energy Services' founding public-company chief executive from the time of its October 2016 NASDAQ IPO — at a price of $15 per share and with an initial market capitalisation of roughly $750 million — through December 31, 2024, a tenure of nearly nine years that encompassed essentially every major chapter in the company's history. Under Straehla, Mammoth built out and then saw collapse its pressure-pumping and oilfield services franchises during the 2018–2020 commodity cycle, navigated the acquisition of Cobra Acquisitions LLC and the award of emergency transmission and distribution rebuild contracts in Puerto Rico following Hurricane Maria in September 2017, and then spent the better part of five years managing the PREPA receivables dispute through arbitration and the Puerto Rico municipal bankruptcy proceedings.

Straehla also presided over the early phases of the infrastructure services repositioning — building 5 Star Electric and Higher Power Electrical into businesses generating more than $90 million in annual revenue before those assets were monetised. He served simultaneously as a director of the company throughout his CEO tenure, giving up the board seat alongside the executive role upon his retirement. Board Chairman Arthur Amron, in the November 2024 announcement of Straehla's departure, offered a diplomatic but compact valediction:

> "On behalf of the Board and the entire Mammoth team, I want to thank Arty for his years of service as Mammoth's CEO and Board member and valuable contributions to the Company. We wish him well in his retirement."

Straehla's precise biographical background is not disclosed in detail in public filings, a common characteristic of the founder-adjacent executives who emerged from Wexford's portfolio company ecosystem in the mid-2010s.

## Phil Lancaster: Succession and Departure

Phil Lancaster's six-month tenure as chief executive — January 1 through June 30, 2025 — was among the briefest in Mammoth's public history, but the transactions completed under his watch were among the most consequential. Lancaster, aged 68 at the time of appointment, brought more than two decades of oilfield services executive experience spanning companies that were themselves Wexford-adjacent: he served as CEO of Great White Energy Services from 2006 to 2010, consulted for Wexford Capital LP directly in 2010 and 2011, and then ran Redback Energy Services as CEO from 2011 to 2015 before joining Mammoth as President of Mammoth Energy Partners LP in 2014 and 2015. His most operationally relevant prior role within Mammoth was a brief but critical stint as interim president of Cobra Acquisitions LLC, Higher Power Electrical LLC, and 5 Star Electric LLC from June to November 2019 — precisely the period when PREPA payment shortfalls were becoming acute and the infrastructure subsidiaries required steadying leadership.

Amron described Lancaster's selection to the top job in fulsome terms:

> "We have complete confidence in Phil's capabilities to carry out Mammoth's business strategy and lead Mammoth into the future to unlock further value. Phil has a wealth of experience and knowledge, boasting over 20 years of experience in the energy industry that includes senior leadership roles and public board service."

Lancaster's compensation was formalised via an SEC Form 8-K in February 2025: an annual base salary of $350,000 and a monthly bonus of $20,000. The board's subsequent disclosure that he had resigned effective June 30, 2025 — departing alongside the $108.7 million sale of 5 Star Electric, Higher Power Electrical, and Python Equipment to Peak Utility Services Group — made clear that Lancaster had in effect shepherded the infrastructure assets to a buyer and then followed them there, joining Peak Utility Services Group as a vice president. Amron again offered the formal acknowledgement: "On behalf of the Board and the entire Mammoth team, I want to thank Phil for his years of service to Mammoth, most recently as CEO." Lancaster was subsequently appointed a non-independent director effective July 2025, retaining a board seat even as operational authority passed elsewhere. He holds a Bachelor of Science from David Lipscomb College and previously served as a director of Bronco Drilling Company and Gulfport Energy Corporation.

## The Executive Bench: Layton, Bernard Lancaster, and Jacobi

Against the backdrop of CEO turbulence, Mark Layton has provided unusual continuity at the CFO position. Layton joined Mammoth at its formation in June 2016 and remained in post through the frozen snapshot date — a span approaching a decade that encompassed the PREPA receivables crisis, two CEO changes, and the infrastructure divestiture. His background is anchored in oilfield-services finance: prior roles at Stingray Pressure Pumping, Archer Well Company, and Great White Energy Services gave him direct familiarity with the same operating companies that formed the nucleus of Mammoth's initial portfolio. Layton holds a Bachelor of Science in Accounting from the University of Central Oklahoma and is a certified public accountant. His 2025 total disclosed compensation was $560,385.

Bernard Lancaster — notably, a different Lancaster from Phil — was appointed Chief Operating Officer effective July 1, 2025. Aged 37 at the time of appointment, Bernard Lancaster brought more than eleven years of tenure within Mammoth subsidiaries, having previously served as Vice President of Operations and held earlier leadership positions at Stingray Energy Services and Redback Energy Services. His operational experience spans health, safety, and environmental management alongside technical drilling functions. He holds a Bachelor of Business Administration in Finance from St. Edward's University.

Paul Jacobi, 59, assumed the role of Chief Business Officer effective July 1, 2025, the same date as Bernard Lancaster's COO appointment, and has served simultaneously as a non-independent director since July 2020. Jacobi has been a managing director at Wexford Capital LP since 1996, responsible for the firm's private equity energy investments. His pre-Wexford career traced through KPMG in audit, Kidder Peabody in investment banking, and Moody's in financial analysis. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Accounting from Villanova University and is a CPA. As the senior Wexford professional on the executive team and the board simultaneously, Jacobi occupies a role with few precedents in Mammoth's governance history — a position that consolidates investor representation and operational authority in a single person.

## The Board: Wexford's Durable Architecture

The six-member board that stood at the frozen snapshot date carried the imprint of Wexford Capital across three of its seats, in varying degrees of directness. [Arthur Amron](https://ir.mammothenergy.com/corporate-governance/board-of-directors), 69, serves as Chairman and has been a director since January 2019. He joined Wexford in 1994, rose to partner and General Counsel — responsible for all internal legal and securities compliance, and active in bankruptcy and restructuring work — and departed the firm in 2023. Amron holds a J.D. from Harvard Law School and a B.A. in Political Theory from Colgate University. Although he no longer holds a Wexford position as of the frozen date, his 29-year institutional history at the firm and his role as Mammoth's chairman make him the primary articulator of Wexford's governance philosophy on the board.

Paul Jacobi's dual executive-director seat has been noted above. The third Wexford-connected figure is Mark Plaumann, 70, who joined the board in June 2025 as an independent director. Plaumann co-founded Greyhawke Capital Advisors LLC in 1998 after an earlier stint as Senior Vice President at Wexford Capital. His Greyhawke advisory work spans private equity, distressed debt, and energy infrastructure — a profile that brings financial restructuring sophistication directly relevant to Mammoth's capital recycling phase. He simultaneously serves as a director of Diamondback Energy, the Permian Basin pure-play, providing cross-industry perspective. Plaumann holds an M.B.A. and a B.A. in Business Administration from the University of Central Florida.

The three independent directors without Wexford connections bring complementary credentials. James Palm, 81 — the board's longest-serving member since June 2017 — spent the bulk of his career in upstream oil and gas, serving as CEO of Gulfport Energy Corporation from 2005 to 2014 and founding Crescent Exploration LLC. His engineering background (B.S. Mechanical Engineering, Oklahoma State University) and operational depth make him the board's most direct peer to Mammoth's oilfield services heritage. Dr. Corey Booker, 50, joined in August 2020, bringing a distinctly non-energy perspective: he is CEO and founder of Bedside LLC, a healthcare management company, and formerly practised as a maternal fetal medicine specialist at Duke University Hospital. He holds an M.D. from Creighton University and an M.S. in Clinical Informatics from Duke, and chairs the Finance Committee at HarborPath Inc. Phil Lancaster himself rounds out the six as a non-independent director, the only former executive on the board.

## Committee Architecture and Governance Standards

All three standing committees are staffed exclusively by independent directors, satisfying both Nasdaq listing rules and institutional governance expectations. Mark Plaumann chairs the Audit Committee, with Corey Booker and James Palm as members; the role carries a supplemental annual retainer of $10,000 above the $50,000 base paid to all non-employee directors. Arthur Amron chairs the Compensation Committee, joined by Palm and Plaumann. Palm chairs the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, with Amron and Plaumann completing the roster. The board held five formal meetings in 2025 — two in person, three virtual — with full attendance across all sessions.

The company maintains a clawback policy compliant with Nasdaq listing standards and 2023 SEC rules, and offers no employment contracts or guaranteed severance to named executive officers beyond standard change-of-control provisions. The 2024 Equity Incentive Plan governs long-term compensation, with restricted stock units typically vesting over three to four years. Total non-employee director remuneration runs to approximately $55,000–$65,000 annually depending on committee assignments — a relatively modest structure for a NASDAQ-listed services company, consistent with Mammoth's small-cap profile and Wexford's historically conservative approach to governance overhead.
