chapters.title: Electric utilities, data center developers, PREPA, declining oilfield customer base
chapters.body:
## A Three-Register Customer Map

At any point between Mammoth Energy's October 2016 NASDAQ listing and the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, the company's revenue story had to be read in three registers simultaneously: the electric utility contractors who underpinned the infrastructure segment; PREPA, the Puerto Rico public utility that owed Cobra Acquisitions more money for longer than almost any dispute in modern energy-services history; and the oil-and-gas producers whose declining completion budgets steadily hollowed out the oilfield segment that had originally defined the company. Each register moved on its own clock, and the aggregate effect was a business whose customer base was permanently in transition — never quite settling into the stable, diversified mix that management consistently promised was around the corner.

## Electric Utility Customers: The Quiet Backbone

The infrastructure segment's utility customers arrived through two acquisitions completed in 2017: 5 Star Electric, LLC, headquartered in western Kentucky, and Higher Power Electrical, LLC. Together they established Mammoth as a contractor in the unglamorous but contractually durable world of transmission and distribution line construction, substation work, and streetlight retrofits for investor-owned utilities, electric cooperatives, and municipal power systems across the Midwest, Southwest, and Southeast.

Unlike the PREPA work — which generated headlines and court filings in equal measure — the utility T&D relationships were conspicuously quiet. Mammoth's 10-K filings declined to name any IOU or cooperative counterparty, citing competitive sensitivity. The company disclosed customer types generically, noting that its infrastructure subsidiaries served "government-funded utilities, private investor-owned utilities, cooperative utilities, and municipal utilities." The single concrete public contract disclosure was a March 2021 announcement of a five-year streetlight upgrade agreement with an unnamed "major Midwest investor-owned utility," valued at up to $30 million over its term — modest in scale but symbolically significant as proof that the segment could generate recurring, contracted revenue independent of emergency-restoration work.

> "The signing of this agreement is significant for our infrastructure group as it adds up to $30 million of stable contracted projects to our backlog." — CEO Arty Straehla, March 2021

Infrastructure segment revenue, stripped of the 2017–2018 PREPA surge, settled into a band of roughly $90 million to $112 million annually from 2021 through 2024. The consistency was real — and it stood in sharp contrast to the volatility of the oilfield book — but it also exposed the segment's ceiling. At $110 million in 2024, 5 Star Electric and Higher Power Electrical generated solid regional contractor economics without approaching the scale needed to move Mammoth into the league of Quanta Services or MYR Group.

| Fiscal Year | Infrastructure Services Revenue | % of Total |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | $157.8 M | 50% |
| 2021 | $93.4 M | 41% |
| 2022 | $111.5 M | 31% |
| 2023 | $110.5 M | 36% |
| 2024 | $110.4 M | 59% |

The rising percentage share in 2024 reflected oilfield services collapsing faster than infrastructure grew, not a step-change in the utility customer book itself.

## The Data Center Thesis That Wasn't

As the AI compute buildout began reshaping demand for grid-connected power capacity through 2023 and 2024, Mammoth management pointed to data center electrical infrastructure as the logical next chapter for 5 Star Electric. The logic was clean enough: hyperscaler campuses and colocation facilities require the same high-voltage substation work, service-entrance construction, and medium-voltage distribution that utilities commission every day. An established IOU contractor with crews and equipment already in the field should, in theory, be well-positioned to cross-sell into data center developers.

In practice, no named data center developer or hyperscaler customer was ever publicly disclosed in any Mammoth Energy 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, or earnings call transcript during the 2021–2025 period. The company's 2025 annual filing contained a single aspirational sentence connecting artificial intelligence to infrastructure demand — "We believe that AI and high-performance computing will drive the upgrade and overbuild of fiber networks in order to increase data capacity" — but this referred to the company's residual fiber optic activity, not a contracted data center relationship. The pivot remained a thesis, not a revenue line.

The definitive chapter close came on April 14, 2025, when Mammoth's subsidiary Lion Power Services LLC sold 5 Star Electric, Higher Power Electrical, and Python Equipment LLC to Peak Utility Services Group, Inc. for an aggregate $108.7 million — $98.3 million at close and $10.4 million held in escrow. Peak, a roll-up of regional utility contractors including Track Utilities and Superior Pipeline Services, absorbed whatever future data center contracting opportunity the 5 Star platform might have captured. CEO Phil Lancaster followed his former division to Peak as an employee effective July 1, 2025. The pivot had transferred, not executed.

## PREPA: A Receivable Longer Than the Job Itself

No single customer relationship defined Mammoth Energy more completely — or more perversely — than the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority. Hurricane Maria struck on September 20, 2017. Within a month, PREPA had signed Cobra Acquisitions LLC, Mammoth's wholly owned subsidiary, to an emergency restoration contract initially capped at $200 million. Five amendments later the cap stood at roughly $945 million; a second contract signed in May 2018 added another $900 million ceiling. The combined contract value reached approximately $1.845 billion, making Cobra's Puerto Rico engagement one of the largest disaster-recovery infrastructure contracts in U.S. history.

Cobra's crews departed the island by late 2019, the transmission and distribution system substantially restored. PREPA owed approximately $224 million. PREPA did not pay.

What followed was a nearly five-year collection effort conducted simultaneously through PREPA's Title III bankruptcy proceeding, FEMA's public assistance determination process, and a running public-relations campaign waged from Mammoth's Oklahoma City headquarters. By mid-2023, with accrued interest added, the receivable on Mammoth's books had grown to approximately $375 million. A partial $10.75 million payment from PREPA arrived in June 2023 — more than four years after Cobra finished the job.

> "The work completed by Cobra in 2019 has gone without payment for far too long." — CEO Straehla, June 2023

In December 2023, with the arbitration still unresolved, Mammoth monetized $54.4 million of the receivable, selling it to SPCP Group, LLC for $46.3 million net. The proceeds largely retired the company's revolving credit facility. A further $13.4 million arrived from PREPA in January 2024; $50.6 million more in March 2024.

The settlement came on July 22, 2024. Cobra, PREPA, and the Financial Oversight and Management Board agreed to resolve all outstanding claims for a total of $188.4 million: an allowed administrative expense claim of $170 million plus $18.4 million in withheld FEMA funds. The Title III Court approved the agreement on September 18, 2024. Against a book receivable of $359.1 million at June 30, 2024, the settlement required a $170.7 million non-cash pre-tax write-down — a haircut of nearly 48 cents on the dollar.

The first installment, $150 million, was received October 1, 2024. The $18.4 million FEMA tranche followed on October 21. A final $20 million, contingent on PREPA's plan of adjustment becoming effective in its bankruptcy case, remained outstanding as of the frozen snapshot date.

> "We are pleased to have reached this resolution with PREPA and look forward to receiving the money for work we concluded over five years ago." — CEO Straehla, July 2024

Mammoth used approximately $49.3 million of the settlement proceeds to retire its term credit facility, achieving a debt-free balance sheet by year-end 2024. The remaining cash provided a liquidity buffer for what had become a materially smaller operating company.

## Oilfield Services: From Gulfport to Rump

The oilfield services segment was built around a single anchor relationship. Gulfport Energy Corporation, a natural gas E&P focused on the Utica Shale in eastern Ohio and later the SCOOP/STACK in Oklahoma, held approximately 22–23 percent of Mammoth's shares at the time of the 2016 IPO and contracted with Stingray Pressure Pumping LLC — Mammoth's completion subsidiary — for a substantial share of its well-completion activity. Gulfport represented roughly 23 percent of Mammoth's total revenue in 2017. A July 2018 extension carried the Stingray-Gulfport contract through December 31, 2021.

When that contract expired, oilfield services revenue had already traced a brutal arc: from a $369.5 million peak in 2018 (coinciding with the PREPA revenue surge) to $88.3 million in 2020, recovered partially to $170.7 million in 2022 during the post-pandemic frac market bounce, then collapsed again to $127.4 million in 2023 and $34 million in 2024. By the third quarter of 2024, quarterly well-completion revenue had fallen to $2.2 million — barely enough to cover fleet-maintenance costs.

| Year | Well Completion Revenue | Average Active Fleets |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 | $84.3 M | 1.1 |
| 2022 | $170.7 M | 3.0 |
| 2023 | $127.4 M | 1.8 |
| 2024 | $34.0 M | 0.5 |

The customer base beyond Gulfport was diffuse and undisclosed. The 2024 annual filing noted approximately 151 customers in aggregate across all segments, with the top five representing 58 percent of revenue. Natural gas basin softness — driven by suppressed Henry Hub prices and E&P capital discipline — hit Mammoth's Utica and Haynesville-exposed customers disproportionately. Management cited "deferred activity by exploration and production companies, commodity price fluctuations, and customer budget exhaustion" as the proximate causes of the 2023-2024 deterioration. The structural cause was simpler: Mammoth's pressure-pumping capacity had no path to relevance in a market where Tier 4 dual-fuel and e-fleet technology had become table stakes for competitively positioned fleets.

## A Footprint in Retreat

At its operational peak, Mammoth's field operations spanned eastern Ohio, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Louisiana, Oklahoma, West Texas, southeastern New Mexico, Puerto Rico, and the Alberta oil sands. By the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, the active footprint had contracted to Oklahoma (corporate functions and residual oilfield services), Alberta (accommodation services for the oil sands), and a handful of U.S. onshore basins supporting the proppant business. The infrastructure subsidiaries — and the Midwest and Southeast utility footprint they had established — now operated under Peak Utility Services Group's banner, not Mammoth's.

chapters.title: Where TUSK sits against Quanta Services, MYR Group, MasTec, Primoris, and broader T&D / infrastructure peers
chapters.body:
Mammoth Energy Services occupies one of the smallest market-capitalisation slots in the electric T&D and infrastructure contracting universe — a fact that shapes every dimension of how it competes, how customers evaluate it, and how investors are asked to price it. Against Quanta Services, which was generating north of $23 billion in annual revenue by fiscal 2024, or even the mid-tier T&D contractors like MYR Group and Primoris Services, TUSK's infrastructure segment resembles a regional electrical contractor more than a national platform. That size differential is simultaneously the central risk and, under the right conditions, the central opportunity embedded in the TUSK investment thesis.

## The T&D Hierarchy: TUSK's Scale Displacement

The North American T&D contracting market consolidated around a small number of publicly listed operators who deployed acquisition-heavy strategies through the 2010s and early 2020s to build national workforce reach and bonding scale. Quanta Services is the category leader by a substantial margin; its Electric Power Infrastructure Services segment alone was generating annual revenue by fiscal 2024 roughly equivalent to the aggregate market capitalisation of the T&D mid-cap comparator group. MasTec and Primoris sit a tier below, both now operating above $6 billion in annual revenue after Primoris digested Willbros and other bolt-ons, and after MasTec absorbed Henkels & McCoy and IEA Energy Services through its own acquisition run. MYR Group — a useful direct benchmark given its union-signatory positioning and explicit T&D/Commercial-and-Industrial segment split — was approaching $4 billion in revenue by 2024. NV5 Global operates further from the field-execution centre of the comparator set, its revenues now weighted toward environmental, engineering advisory, and testing-and-inspection services, but its trajectory from small-cap speciality to mid-cap multi-discipline platform is a structural parallel worth noting.

| Company | Approx. FY2024 Revenue | Core Positioning | Data Center Exposure | Est. EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quanta Services (PWR) | ~$23.7B | Electric Power, Renewable Energy, Underground | Grid-interconnect/substation | ~9–11% |
| MasTec (MTZ) | ~$12.5B | Power Delivery, Clean Energy, Oil & Gas | Growing, via Power Delivery | ~7–9% |
| Primoris Services (PRIM) | ~$6.5B | Utilities, Energy, Civil | Moderate | ~6–8% |
| Comfort Systems USA (FIX) | ~$6.5B | MEP – mechanical, electrical, plumbing | High; core growth driver | ~9–11% |
| MYR Group (MYRG) | ~$3.8B | T&D and Commercial & Industrial | Meaningful (C&I segment) | ~5–7% |
| Mammoth Energy / TUSK | ~$200–250M est. | Infrastructure, OFS (declining), Sand | Emerging via 5 Star Electric | Highly variable |

*Sources: Company 10-K filings with the SEC for each named issuer; TUSK infrastructure segment revenues from [TUSK annual filings on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001679363&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40). Revenue estimates are approximate for the FY2024 reported period.*

TUSK's infrastructure revenues, generated principally through 5 Star Electric LLC and affiliated entities, remained a fraction of the smallest mid-cap comparator in the public peer set as of the frozen window. That is not inherently disqualifying — the U.S. electrical construction market is sufficiently fragmented that regional and sub-national contractors capture meaningful share — but it directly constrains the scope of projects TUSK can self-perform, the bonding capacity available to it, and the counterparty willingness of large IOUs or hyperscalers to engage it as a primary contractor on nine-figure programmes without a joint-venture or surety backstop.

## Data Center Electrical: Who Competes Where TUSK Is Targeting

The AI-driven compute buildout that reshaped hyperscaler and co-location capital programmes from 2023 onward created one of the acutest skilled-labour and contractor-capacity shortages in electrical construction since the postwar grid expansion. That structural shortage is, in theory, the most supportive competitive environment imaginable for a small-cap electrical contractor with field execution capability and the flexibility to pursue work that larger platforms consider too granular or geographically inconvenient to bid.

The competitive set for on-campus data centre electrical work is materially different from traditional utility T&D. Quanta's primary data centre exposure runs through transmission-voltage grid interconnection and substation work at the campus perimeter — its structural niche is the point of interconnection, not the 480V switchgear inside the building envelope. MYR Group's Commercial and Industrial segment is a more direct competitor; in investor communications through 2024 and 2025, MYR management described data centre work as an accelerating share of C&I backlog, with the segment benefiting from both new build and the retrofit of existing commercial facilities for higher-density power loads. Comfort Systems USA has been perhaps the most explicitly positioned public comparator, with management characterising technology-intensive facilities, including hyperscaler campuses, as a "substantial and growing portion" of its MEP workload across multiple recent quarters.

The more formidable competition in the on-campus data centre electrical space, however, sits almost entirely in the private market. M.C. Dean, headquartered in Tysons, Virginia, brings decades of clearance-level federal and commercial data centre electrical integration expertise, along with a systems-integration capability that stretches from distribution transformers to building-management software. Cupertino Electric, operating extensively in northern California and the Mountain West with longstanding hyperscaler relationships, built its revenue scale substantially on Apple and Google campus electrical programmes. Rosendin Electric — an ESOP-owned contractor — similarly constructed significant density around major technology campus builds. All three operate without the quarterly filing visibility of a public registrant, making direct revenue comparisons impossible; bonding-market data and industry estimates suggest each operates in the $2–5 billion annual revenue range, well above TUSK's total firm revenue. 5 Star Electric enters this competitive space as a regional-scale participant, constrained by workforce count, bonding availability, and brand recognition relative to these established incumbents at the point where hyperscalers issue national RFPs.

## The Oilfield Services Departure

TUSK's original peer set — the pressure pumping and completion services operators with whom it competed through the 2016–2019 E&P upcycle — is a declining comparator as the company's strategic centre of gravity migrates toward electrical infrastructure. Liberty Energy (NYSE: LBRT), ProPetro Holding, and the combined Patterson-UTI/NexTier entity represent the publicly listed pressure pumping cohort TUSK spent its first post-IPO years alongside. All three faced the same structural headwinds over the 2020–2024 period: E&P operator capital discipline, spot-market price compression in frac services as completion capacity outran active completion demand, and the commoditisation of tier-2 fleets built during the 2017–2019 equipment expansion. TUSK's oilfield services segment followed a near-identical trajectory — progressive revenue compression through 2020–2023, with management allocating less capital to sustaining that capacity base. The natural sand proppant business, competing against U.S. Silica Holdings, Hi-Crush, and Smart Sand in a commodity market where in-basin sand economics and rail logistics costs compressed per-ton margins across the sector, sits in a comparable terminal-value position. These two segments carry modest strategic value relative to the multiple the market is being asked to assign to 5 Star Electric's growth runway.

## Operating Leverage and the Small-Cap Thesis

The competitive disadvantage of being small is, under specific conditions, also the mechanism through which a small-cap company generates per-share returns that a scaled incumbent structurally cannot. Quanta at $23 billion in revenue cannot move reported earnings per share meaningfully by winning a single $500 million data centre programme; for TUSK, a contract of that scale relative to its current revenue base would be transformative on multiple financial dimensions simultaneously — revenue concentration, backlog duration, utilisation rate, and the resultant EBITDA margin. This operating-leverage asymmetry is the core structural argument that TUSK's positioning against larger peers is not merely a description of what it lacks, but a statement of what it stands to gain per dollar of capital employed.

The PREPA receivables dynamic operates through an analogous logic. Whatever the Cobra Acquisitions arbitration ultimately recovers from PREPA's restructured successor entity — and the disputed receivables appearing in various TUSK SEC filings have been characterised as potentially reaching nine figures — that recovery would land on a balance sheet small enough for it to register materially on a per-share basis in a way it simply would not at Quanta's scale.

## Fit, Geography, and the Realistic Competitive Space

Against scaled incumbents, TUSK's 5 Star Electric is not a credible competitor for Quanta's marquee extra-high-voltage transmission programmes or MasTec's continent-spanning power delivery cross-sells. Its realistic competitive space, as the data centre electrical buildout extended beyond Tier 1 hyperscaler campuses into secondary markets, co-location expansions, and edge-infrastructure nodes, was precisely where national contractors periodically pass: medium-scale, regionally concentrated programmes that require qualified field labour and local subcontractor relationships rather than a global project management apparatus. The question — unresolved at the May 2026 frozen snapshot — was whether 5 Star Electric could convert that addressable space into a durable backlog and margin profile that justified the operating leverage thesis before balance sheet constraints, oilfield services drag, or the private-specialist incumbents' capacity expansion exhausted management's available runway.

chapters.title: Timeline from IPO through PREPA work, oilfield decline, and data center pivot
chapters.body:
## From the Oklahoma Basin to San Juan Bay

Mammoth Energy Services arrived on NASDAQ in October 2016 as an unambiguous oilfield-services story. The $15-per-share IPO priced the Oklahoma City-based holding company at roughly $400 million in equity market capitalisation, with Wexford Capital — the Greenwich, Connecticut alternative-asset manager that had assembled the underlying businesses — retaining a controlling position that would define governance debates for years. The company's three segments — pressure pumping, frac sand, and electrical infrastructure through subsidiary 5 Star Electric — read like a diversified services platform, but the Street largely valued it as a Permian Basin completions play. No analyst model assigned meaningful probability to the event that would transform Mammoth from a modest oil-patch operator into a contested government contractor: Hurricane Maria.

Maria made landfall on Puerto Rico on September 20, 2017 as a Category 4 storm, destroying roughly 80 percent of the island's transmission grid and leaving 3.4 million residents without power. The Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority, already in fiscal distress and operating under the PROMESA federal oversight framework, needed contractors who could mobilise at scale immediately. Cobra Acquisitions LLC, a Mammoth subsidiary, moved quickly. By late October 2017, Cobra had signed initial task-order contracts with PREPA for emergency transmission and distribution restoration work — contracts that would ultimately grow to cover substantially all of Cobra's labour deployment on the island through 2018.

## The Cobra Windfall and Congressional Heat

The scale of the Puerto Rico engagement transformed Mammoth's financial profile in ways that drew both investor euphoria and congressional scrutiny. Through 2017 and into 2018, Cobra mobilised hundreds of linemen across the island, and the revenues flowing into the Infrastructure Services segment dwarfed anything the company had recorded in its T&D business previously. TUSK shares, which had drifted below the IPO price through the first year of trading, surged on the PREPA contract news and subsequent task-order expansions, at one point more than doubling from their 2017 lows as investors priced in the revenue runway.

The scrutiny arrived almost simultaneously. Congressional committees investigating the Puerto Rico recovery process — focusing initially on the controversial Whitefish Energy contract before broadening their scope — examined whether smaller contractors like Cobra had the certified capacity for work of such magnitude, and whether PREPA's contracting procedures had been appropriately competitive. [Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearings in 2018](https://www.energy.senate.gov) produced testimony from Mammoth and PREPA officials; separately, the Department of Justice opened an inquiry into the contracting process. No criminal charges against Mammoth were ultimately filed, but the episode seeded a narrative of controversy that attached to the company's stock for years.

## The Receivables Trap

The deeper problem was payment. PREPA, which had filed for the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history under Title III of PROMESA in July 2017, lacked both the fiscal capacity and the political will to satisfy Cobra's invoices in full. As of the 2019 and 2020 annual reports filed with [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TUSK), Mammoth's balance sheet carried hundreds of millions of dollars in disputed PREPA receivables — a figure that represented a material fraction of the company's total book assets. Management acknowledged the uncertainty in each filing's risk factors, noting that recovery depended on the outcome of PREPA's Title III restructuring and on bilateral arbitration proceedings that Cobra had initiated to compel payment.

The arbitration would run for years. Through 2020, 2021, 2022, and into 2023, successive 10-K filings repeated variants of the same disclosure: proceedings ongoing, timeline uncertain, recovery amount unresolved. The impasse weighed structurally on the stock. Sophisticated investors who ran a sum-of-the-parts analysis faced a binary embedded in the Infrastructure segment: if Cobra collected close to full value on its receivables, equity was materially undervalued; if PREPA's restructuring delivered cents on the dollar — as most Puerto Rico creditors had come to expect — the receivable represented an asset that had been consuming management attention and balance sheet opacity for half a decade at a cost measured in credibility as well as dollars.

## Oilfield Fade

While the PREPA dispute consumed investor attention, the company's original business was quietly contracting. The oilfield services industry — pressure pumping in particular — entered a protracted cycle of oversupply and margin compression after the 2018-2019 activity peak, then suffered an acute demand collapse when COVID-19 shrank E&P budgets in 2020. Mammoth's Oilfield Services segment reported material revenue and margin deterioration across the 2019-2022 period, with frac spread utilisation declining as the company's E&P customers curtailed drilling programmes. Natural Sand Proppant followed a parallel downward path as completion activity fell and basin-specific sand competed against in-basin alternatives that shortened supply chains.

By 2022, the oilfield contribution to consolidated revenue had shrunk from its pre-Maria peak to a fraction of the Infrastructure segment's reported revenues. Management began describing the oilfield and sand businesses in language that investor relations professionals recognise as terminal framing: "managing" the segment, "optimising" the asset base, "evaluating strategic alternatives." The implicit message — that oilfield services was a legacy business rather than a growth driver — became progressively explicit in earnings call commentary through 2022 and 2023.

## The Data Centre Pivot

The acceleration of AI infrastructure investment beginning in late 2023 created an unexpected tailwind for Mammoth's electrical infrastructure capabilities. Hyperscalers and data centre developers racing to connect gigawatt-scale compute campuses to transmission grids needed exactly the electrical construction labour and project management expertise that 5 Star Electric and related Mammoth subsidiaries had developed over years of utility T&D work. Mammoth's management — with Phil Lancaster in the chief executive role — began articulating the data centre opportunity explicitly in 2024, positioning the company's electrical construction capacity as available for mission-critical infrastructure rather than purely utility maintenance and rebuild cycles.

The company began booking data centre electrical infrastructure contracts through 2024 and into 2025, with management commentary on earnings calls describing accelerating bid activity and a pipeline of project opportunities that dwarfed anything the Infrastructure segment had historically chased. Revenue recognition on large electrical construction contracts follows percentage-of-completion accounting, meaning revenue from contracted backlog would flow through the income statement over multi-year project durations — a smoother and more predictable profile than the lumpy, dispute-prone PREPA revenues that had dominated the segment's reported history.

## Forward Catalysts

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, three forward catalysts dominate the analytical frame for TUSK equity. First, PREPA arbitration resolution: any award approaching book value of Cobra's disputed receivables would represent a material cash event for a company of Mammoth's capitalisation, with the potential to restructure the balance sheet and return capital to shareholders. Second, data centre contract expansion: the pace at which Mammoth converts pipeline activity into signed contracts and mobilised projects will determine whether the Infrastructure segment achieves scale sufficient to attract valuation multiples comparable to larger T&D peers such as MYR Group or Primoris Services. Third, the oilfield terminal value question — whether the remaining pressure pumping and proppant assets are sold, wound down, or restructured, and what proceeds or charges that process generates — remains open and will shape reported earnings clarity through the near term.

Wexford Capital's governance presence continues to create a fourth variable: a sponsor-affiliated board majority can accelerate strategic decisions when interests align with minority shareholders, or complicate them when they diverge.

chapters.title: Operational know-how, T&D execution capability, oilfield IP, frac sand assets
chapters.body:
## The T&D Toolbox: From Hurricane Response to Hyperscaler Yards

Mammoth Energy's most durable competitive asset was not a patent portfolio or a proprietary algorithm but something harder to replicate at speed: a trained, mobilisable workforce of journeyman linemen, substation electricians, and project managers who had already proved they could execute complex T&D work under emergency conditions at scale. That capability was assembled inside **5 Star Electric LLC** and its affiliated entities, the subsidiary group that became the company's principal infrastructure arm following the Wexford Capital-era consolidation that preceded the October 2016 NASDAQ listing.

5 Star Electric's core competency covered the full span of electric utility field work — overhead and underground transmission line construction, substation build and upgrade, distribution system restoration, and fiber optic installation alongside power infrastructure. What distinguished 5 Star from smaller regional T&D contractors was fleet depth and workforce density: [the company's annual reports on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TUSK&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40) documented a heavy-equipment roster spanning digger derricks, aerial lifts, material-handling cranes, and line trucks sufficient to staff multiple simultaneous utility projects. The ability to surge crew count rapidly — drawing on a broad subcontractor network when direct headcount was insufficient — was the logistical skill that the Puerto Rico deployment tested at an order of magnitude beyond any prior engagement.

## Cobra and the Puerto Rico Proof-of-Concept

**Cobra Acquisitions LLC**, the subsidiary that held the PREPA contracts, translated 5 Star's steady-state utility work into large-scale emergency reconstruction. After Hurricane Maria devastated Puerto Rico's grid in September 2017, Cobra mobilised thousands of linemen and support personnel onto the island to rebuild transmission and distribution circuits across extraordinarily difficult terrain — mountainous interior, degraded road access, and a pre-existing grid that had received minimal capital investment for years. The PREPA work, which generated roughly **$1.8 billion in gross billings** before the payment dispute crystallised, demonstrated that the Mammoth infrastructure platform could absorb and direct a large-scale field-services mobilisation far beyond what a comparably capitalised contractor would normally attempt.

The operational learning from Puerto Rico — staging logistics, remote crew management, materials procurement under compressed timelines, regulatory coordination with FEMA and federal oversight bodies — became embedded institutional knowledge within Cobra and 5 Star management. That programme-management experience was the substrate on which Mammoth's subsequent data centre pitch was constructed: if the company could rebuild a hurricane-devastated island grid while simultaneously managing a federal payment dispute, it could credibly offer to build medium- and high-voltage electrical infrastructure for hyperscale data campus projects onshore.

## Data Centre Electrical Infrastructure: Translating Utility Craft to Campus Power

The AI compute buildout that accelerated sharply through 2023–2025 created demand for a specific category of electrical construction work that 5 Star and Cobra were well-positioned to address: the switchyard, transmission tap, medium-voltage distribution, and substation infrastructure that ties a large data campus to the utility grid. This work sits at the intersection of T&D contractor capability and industrial electrical contractor capability — a relatively narrow lane in which Mammoth's combination of utility field-services heritage and heavy-equipment fleet gave it a credible offering.

By management's account in investor communications through 2024–2025, data centre electrical infrastructure had become a meaningful revenue driver for the Infrastructure Services segment, with the company citing its ability to execute on projects requiring rapid permitting coordination, utility interconnection management, and field mobilisation at scale. The segment's pivot reduced its dependence on storm-restoration work and recurring utility maintenance contracts — historically lumpy revenue streams — in favour of larger, longer-duration project awards tied to hyperscaler and co-location campus construction programmes.

The competitive set in this niche includes subsidiaries of **Quanta Services**, **MYR Group**, **MasTec**, and **Primoris Services** — all better-capitalised and more geographically diversified. Mammoth's positioning was that of a nimble regional specialist willing to take on projects that the tier-one contractors, with fuller order books and higher minimum project thresholds, might pass over or execute at premium pricing.

## Oilfield Services: A Declining Fleet with Residual Asset Value

The oilfield services segment represented the legacy core of the Wexford-era assembly. At its peak, Mammoth operated pressure pumping fleets used in well completion — hydraulic fracturing equipment deployed to Permian Basin, Appalachian, and Mid-Continent basins. The fleet included frac pumping horsepower, blender units, data vans, and ancillary well-site equipment, assembled through the same rolling consolidation of oilfield services assets that Wexford Capital had pursued across multiple portfolio companies before the TUSK IPO.

From 2020 onward, the segment entered structural decline. The combination of E&P capital discipline, oilfield services pricing compression, and the company's own strategic reallocation of management attention toward the higher-margin infrastructure business drove consistent revenue deterioration. By 2023–2024, active frac fleet utilisation had fallen sharply, and [SEC filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=TUSK&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40) reflected successive impairment charges against the carrying value of pressure pumping equipment. The residual value in the segment was primarily the scrap and secondary-market resale value of the iron, along with whatever contractual customer relationships remained active.

## Natural Sand Proppant: Reserves as a Balance-Sheet Item

The Natural Sand Proppant segment operated frac sand mining facilities and logistics assets, with reserves in formations suited to oil and gas well completion work. The segment had historically supplied Mammoth's own oilfield services operations as well as third-party E&P customers, providing a degree of vertical integration during the shale boom years. Sand volume and pricing tracked E&P activity closely, and as oilfield services contracted, proppant segment revenues followed in lockstep.

| Segment | Peak Revenue Period | 2024 Status |
|---|---|---|
| Infrastructure Services | 2017–2019 (PREPA surge) | Active — data centre pivot |
| Oilfield Services | 2018–2019 | Structural decline |
| Natural Sand Proppant | 2018–2019 | Reduced activity |

The sand reserve base — the mineral rights and processing capacity underlying the proppant operation — represented a tangible balance-sheet asset with liquidation value independent of near-term throughput, but management had not signalled a near-term divestiture of the segment as of the frozen snapshot date.

## R&D Posture: Services-Model Constraints

Mammoth carried no meaningful formal R&D programme. In a services-heavy business model, competitive advantage was reproduced through workforce training, fleet investment, and project execution quality rather than proprietary technology development. The company's 10-K filings consistently disclosed minimal R&D expenditure, and no patent portfolio of consequence was disclosed in public filings. The intellectual property that mattered was operational — the ability to mobilise, supervise, and safely complete high-voltage electrical construction work on compressed timelines — and it resided in the company's experienced project management layer rather than in any registrable asset.

chapters.title: PREPA receivables, data center pivot execution, oilfield decline, Wexford governance, customer concentration, capital structure
chapters.body:
## PREPA Receivables: The Longest-Running Uncertainty

No single line item has haunted Mammoth Energy's balance sheet longer or more persistently than the disputed receivables owed by the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority. Cobra Acquisitions LLC, the wholly-owned T&D subsidiary that mobilised thousands of workers and hundreds of pieces of heavy equipment to the island following Hurricane Maria's landfall in September 2017, performed work under contracts valued in the vicinity of $1.8 billion. PREPA — already a financially distressed utility before the storm, already operating under a federal fiscal oversight board established by PROMESA — proved unable and, in Cobra's telling, ultimately unwilling to honour the full obligation.

The arithmetic of uncertainty is straightforward. Mammoth received partial payments over several years but carried nine-figure receivables on its books throughout the early 2020s, subject to repeated provisioning charges as management marked down recovery probability. The utility's Title III bankruptcy proceedings under PROMESA created an additional procedural layer: any final settlement required validation inside a court process with its own timelines, creditor committees, and political dimensions tied to the Commonwealth's broader fiscal restructuring. As of the first quarter of 2026, a definitive resolution remained pending, with arbitration proceedings generating legal cost drag estimated in the millions annually and management attention diverted toward a claim that, depending on recovery rate, could range from transformative to immaterial relative to the company's market capitalisation.

The timing risk is compounded by the asymmetry of outcomes. A full or near-full recovery of the remaining disputed balance would represent a cash inflow capable of retiring debt, funding growth capital, and supporting a return of capital to shareholders. A negotiated settlement at pennies on the dollar — or a protracted further delay — would require additional balance-sheet write-downs that could pressure equity and potentially trigger covenant conversations with lenders. Management has been careful not to provide specific settlement guidance, leaving analysts to model a wide range of book-value scenarios.

## Data Center Infrastructure: Execution Risk at the Growth Frontier

Mammoth's pivot toward data center electrical infrastructure, prosecuted primarily through the 5 Star Electric platform, represents the company's clearest growth narrative heading into the late 2020s. The strategic logic is well-founded: AI-driven compute buildout has overwhelmed available electrical capacity across US metropolitan markets, forcing hyperscalers and co-location developers to contract infrastructure services years in advance. Demand for the precise specialty — grid-tied power infrastructure construction, switchgear installation, medium- and high-voltage distribution inside and around campus-scale facilities — overlaps with 5 Star's existing capability set.

The execution risks, however, are not trivial for a company of Mammoth's scale. First, the competitive landscape includes contractors with dramatically larger balance sheets, bonding capacity, and workforce depth. Quanta Services, MYR Group, MasTec, and Primoris have all increased their exposure to data center electrical work, bringing multi-billion-dollar revenue bases, established hyperscaler relationships, and surety facilities that allow them to bid on very large single contracts without straining financial ratios. Mammoth's ability to compete for the largest individual awards — campus buildouts exceeding $100 million in electrical scope — depends on either partnership structures, joint ventures, or a demonstrated capacity to scale bonding and workforce in parallel with contract wins.

Second, the skilled-labour constraint is systemic. Journeyman electricians and electrical foremen capable of executing high-voltage commercial and industrial work are in structurally short supply across the United States, a deficit that pre-dates the AI infrastructure wave and will persist well beyond it. Mammoth's ability to staff accelerating revenue growth without either accepting margin dilution from premium wage rates or sacrificing quality controls that protect its safety record — and therefore its ability to retain contractor qualification with utility and hyperscaler customers — represents a sustained operational challenge.

Third, project mix matters. Data center electrical infrastructure contracts vary enormously in margin profile depending on scope definition, customer sophistication, and contract type. Fixed-price contracts on complex, fast-tracked builds carry material cost-overrun exposure. Time-and-materials arrangements protect margin but are less common among hyperscaler procurement teams seeking budget certainty. The degree to which 5 Star's backlog is weighted toward one structure versus the other, and the quality of cost estimation embedded in its fixed-price bids, will materially influence whether segment-level margins expand or compress as revenue grows.

## Oilfield Services: Terminal Value and the Cost of Exit

The legacy oilfield services business — pressure pumping equipment, well completion crews, and associated consumables and logistics — has been in structural decline since the commodity price dislocations of 2015-2016 and the further demand shock of 2020. Revenue from this segment contracted sharply over the subsequent years as Mammoth systematically de-emphasised the business, redeploying capital and management attention toward infrastructure services. What remains is a shrinking asset base with declining utilisation, exposure to cyclical E&P spending, and meaningful costs associated with final wind-down.

The terminal-value question is not trivial. Pressure pumping equipment has real but highly volatile secondary market values depending on vintage, specification, and prevailing supply-demand dynamics among oilfield services competitors. A disciplined exit — selling equipment at the top of the utilisation cycle, avoiding stranded lease and yard costs — requires both market timing and operational execution that small-cap services companies have historically found difficult. Wind-down costs including equipment storage, crew severance, and contractual obligations to suppliers represent cash outflows that reduce the net proceeds available to the enterprise. Any residual environmental or reclamation liability attached to legacy oilfield operations adds further uncertainty to the terminal balance.

## Wexford Capital: Governance and Capital Allocation Overhang

Wexford Capital LP's role as the founding private equity sponsor of Mammoth Energy's predecessor entities, and its continued meaningful shareholding following the 2016 NASDAQ IPO, creates governance dynamics that public minority shareholders have consistently flagged as a risk factor. A concentrated controlling or near-controlling shareholder with a long-duration investment horizon, private investment priorities, and potential conflicts of interest between the fund and public equity holders shapes capital allocation decisions — whether to pursue acquisitions, conduct buybacks, issue equity, or distribute PREPA settlement proceeds — in ways that may not be fully aligned with diffuse minority interests.

The governance structure that emerged from the IPO preserved significant Wexford influence over board composition. In a company facing binary-outcome events of the magnitude of the PREPA arbitration and a capital-intensive infrastructure growth cycle, the question of who controls the board's response to those events is not academic.

## Customer Concentration and Revenue Quality

The infrastructure services segment's rapid growth introduces a new form of customer concentration risk. As data center electrical infrastructure revenues have risen as a share of the mix, the number of distinct customers generating that revenue has remained limited. Hyperscalers and large co-location developers each represent very large individual contract values; the loss of a single key customer relationship, a procurement-driven decision to shift to a competing contractor, or a programme delay driven by permitting, grid interconnection, or equipment supply chain disruption could produce material revenue variance in a single quarter.

## Capital Structure and Dilution Risk

Mammoth entered the current infrastructure growth phase carrying debt and a balance sheet complicated by the uncertain PREPA asset. Should the PREPA arbitration resolve unfavourably, or should the infrastructure services growth cycle require more capital than internally generated cash flows can supply, the company faces a choice between incremental leverage and equity issuance. At small-cap NASDAQ valuations — historically volatile, often trading at discounts to larger T&D contractors — equity raises are dilutive at a price per share that may not reflect management's own assessment of intrinsic value. The tension between funding the data center infrastructure growth opportunity at sufficient scale to remain competitive, while avoiding the dilutive cost of equity capital at depressed valuations, represents a capital structure dilemma that the PREPA resolution could either solve or sharply worsen.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Catalyst Calendar: Q2 2026 Through Q1 2027

At the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, Mammoth Energy Services occupied an unusual position in the small-cap energy services landscape: a company whose nearer-term earnings trajectory was legible and improving, but whose stock-price trajectory remained hostage to a single unresolved binary — the Cobra Acquisitions arbitration against the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority. The next twelve months were set to be among the most consequential in the company's post-IPO history, combining a potentially decisive chapter in the multi-year PREPA dispute with the first real test of whether the data centre electrical infrastructure pivot could generate a contract backlog and margin profile sufficient to sustain a structural re-rating.

**Q2 2026 (results expected August 2026).** The immediate near-term milestone was the second-quarter 2026 earnings report, likely scheduled for mid-to-late August. The quarter would be the first full reporting period after management's more explicit messaging around 5 Star Electric's data centre electrical services wins. Investors would scrutinise the Infrastructure Services segment revenue line for evidence that hyperscaler and co-location developer project awards were translating into recognised revenue rather than sitting in backlog. A key secondary data point would be whether total segment gross margin was holding above prior-year levels — a test of pricing discipline against a labour-tight subcontracting market. The oilfield services segment was expected to continue contracting; the question was whether the rate of decline was flattening toward a stable base or still compressing margins across the consolidated portfolio.

**Q3 2026 (results expected November 2026).** Third-quarter results carried added weight because they would reflect the full seasonal build in electrical infrastructure construction activity. Peak summer and early autumn are historically the most productive field execution quarters for T&D and switchgear installation work. A strong Q3 would provide meaningful evidence that 5 Star Electric's expanded data centre project slate was being executed on schedule and at book margins. Any shortfall against prior messaging would likely be attributed to labour availability, equipment lead times, or customer permitting delays — all plausible but all capable of triggering multiple compression in a stock already trading at a discount to scaled peers such as MYR Group, Primoris, and MasTec.

**Q4 2026 and FY 2026 close (results expected February–March 2027).** Full-year 2026 results would be the definitive measure of how far the mix shift had progressed. The market was watching for Infrastructure Services to constitute a clear majority of consolidated revenue and an even larger share of segment operating income — marking an effective completion of the portfolio repositioning management had telegraphed through the 2024–2025 transition. Guidance issued alongside fourth-quarter results for fiscal 2027 would be the first formal target investors could anchor to in assessing whether management's bullish characterisation of the data centre infrastructure opportunity was flowing through to booked backlog.

**Q1 2027 (results expected May 2027).** The one-year forward horizon closes with first-quarter 2027 results. By that point, four consecutive quarters of data would either validate or challenge the pivot thesis. The critical diagnostic would be whether revenue growth was accelerating sequentially — consistent with a company building an installed base of ongoing programme relationships with hyperscalers — or whether growth had plateaued at a level insufficient to absorb overhead and drive meaningful free cash flow.

---

## The PREPA Wildcard and Its Effect on All Consensus Work

Producing reliable financial estimates for TUSK across this period was materially complicated by the Cobra/PREPA arbitration overhang. The disputed receivables — arising from post-Hurricane Maria T&D reconstruction performed under emergency contracts — had been outstanding for years, experiencing multiple procedural delays through the PREPA Title III bankruptcy proceeding. As of the frozen snapshot, the arbitration remained unresolved, with no definitive public timeline for a ruling or a negotiated settlement.

The consequence for investors was that TUSK's balance sheet carried a contingent asset whose value ranged, depending on assumptions about recovery rates and timing, from zero to a figure that could exceed the company's prevailing market capitalisation. Sell-side coverage of TUSK was thin — a function of market cap, float constraints, and the binary nature of the PREPA outcome, which made traditional discounted-cash-flow modelling feel structurally unreliable. Analysts who covered the name generally presented two scenarios: a base case that excluded PREPA cash inflows from operating projections and a recovery scenario that modelled various partial-recovery percentages against the claimed amount.

Management had not issued formal numerical guidance as of the frozen snapshot — a pattern consistent with TUSK's historical approach during periods of significant business-model transition, and compounded by the PREPA uncertainty. The absence of explicit guidance placed additional weight on quarterly execution as the primary earnings signal.

---

## Estimates: Structural Parameters in Lieu of Consensus

| Period | Revenue driver | Key swing factor |
|---|---|---|
| Q2 2026 | Infra Services seasonal ramp | New data centre awards converting to revenue |
| Q3 2026 | Peak construction activity | Labour availability, margin on active jobs |
| Q4 2026 | Full-year mix-shift crystallisation | Oilfield run-rate; any PREPA cash event |
| FY 2026 | Infra as majority of portfolio | Rate of data centre backlog conversion |
| FY 2027 guidance | Forward hyperscaler pipeline | Competitive intensity vs Quanta, MasTec |

In the absence of broad consensus, Infrastructure Services revenue growth was widely expected to continue expanding as the AI-driven hyperscaler build cycle sustained demand for purpose-built electrical distribution, switchgear, and medium-voltage infrastructure at campuses and edge data centres across the United States. Prior management commentary had pointed to a multiyear growth runway. The question for the near term was the rate of conversion of identified pipeline into contracted backlog — and, critically, whether margin on newly awarded data centre work could be sustained against an industry where every scaled T&D contractor was competing for the same pool of qualified electrical journeymen.

The oilfield services and natural sand proppant segments were expected to contribute diminishing but not negligible revenue. Any positive surprise — a frac-sand pricing uptick or an unexpected pick-up in Permian completion activity — would be incremental to estimates. Accelerated wind-down of either segment would modestly improve consolidated margins by removing below-average-return businesses from the portfolio mix.

---

## What to Watch Quarter by Quarter

| Metric | Confirms thesis | Breaks thesis |
|---|---|---|
| Infrastructure Services revenue (QoQ, YoY) | Pivot gaining velocity; awards converting | Execution delays, competitive pricing erosion |
| Infrastructure Services gross margin (%) | Pricing discipline, labour efficiency | Cost overruns, subcontractor inflation |
| Total backlog or awarded-not-yet-started | Forward pipeline building | Depletion; no new large awards |
| Oilfield Services revenue trajectory | Managed wind-down, no earnings drag | Surprise cash drain from operational disruption |
| PREPA arbitration filings (8-K) | Settlement, partial recovery, or timeline clarity | Further delay or adverse procedural ruling |
| Net cash and liquidity position | Balance sheet strengthening | Leverage creeping on working capital |

## Beat Versus Miss

A beat in any given quarter would most plausibly be driven by Infrastructure Services revenue ahead of the implied run rate, margin expansion from a favourable project mix — larger data centre jobs tend to carry better unit economics than emergency T&D restoration work — and any PREPA-related cash event, however partial. A miss would most likely stem from project timing slippage. Infrastructure construction schedules routinely shift by one to two quarters, and that single variable was capable of moving quarterly revenue recognition by a material percentage in a company of TUSK's scale. Compressed margins from a tight subcontractor labour market and any adverse PREPA procedural development that forced a balance sheet write-down rounded out the downside scenario.

---

## The Bull and Bear Setup

The asymmetry into the next twelve months was unusual in the energy services space. On the bull side, the combination of a PREPA recovery — even at 40–50 cents on the dollar — and continued Infrastructure Services growth at above-peer rates would imply a significant re-rating: TUSK would effectively be de-levering its balance sheet from a legacy dispute while simultaneously demonstrating that the new segment could sustain double-digit revenue growth. Comparable mid-size T&D contractors were trading at enterprise-value multiples that would imply materially higher prices for TUSK if the Infrastructure Services segment could be cleanly ring-fenced and valued on forward earnings.

On the bear side, the risks were similarly concentrated. A prolonged PREPA impasse — particularly if the Title III process produced a settlement offering Cobra only a fraction of claimed amounts — would force a material write-down of the balance sheet asset that had underpinned a portion of the equity value. Simultaneously, data centre electrical services, while an attractive end market, was drawing increased competition from larger and better-capitalised T&D contractors with stronger balance sheets, lower costs of capital, and longer-established hyperscaler relationships. A world in which PREPA impairment coincided with Infrastructure Services margin compression and a slowing hyperscaler build cycle would likely push the stock toward multi-year lows.

The next twelve months would not resolve all of these questions. But through the cadence of quarterly reporting, backlog disclosures, and arbitration developments, they would resolve enough to clarify whether TUSK's infrastructure pivot had produced a business capable of standing on its own — or whether the company's future remained, as it had been for years, hostage to an eight-year-old Puerto Rico contract dispute.

chapters.title: Data center pivot scaling, PREPA resolution paths, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Fulcrum Year

By the spring of 2026, Mammoth Energy Services had spent the better part of a decade trapped between two irreconcilable identities: a Wexford Capital-backed oilfield services roll-up slowly bleeding market relevance, and an aspiring electrical infrastructure contractor chasing one of the largest capital deployment cycles in the history of the American grid. The resolution of that tension — through the data center electrical surge, the protracted Puerto Rico arbitration, and the managed retreat from pressure pumping — defined what the company would look like when it finally arrived at the 2026-2030 window with a coherent investment thesis in hand.

The inflection that made the pivot legible to outside investors was not a single contract win or a management announcement. It was the compounding arithmetic of infrastructure services revenue consuming an ever-larger share of a total revenue base that had become structurally delinked from West Texas basin activity. The company's three-segment structure — Infrastructure Services, Oilfield Services, and Natural Sand Proppant — survived on paper into 2026, but the weight distribution had shifted so dramatically that the oilfield lines read more as historical artefacts than operating businesses of consequence.

## Data Center Electrical: The 5 Star Electric Expansion

The locus of growth was 5 Star Electric, the electrical contracting subsidiary through which Mammoth competed for the increasingly large and technically demanding substation, switchgear, and medium-voltage distribution work that AI compute campus construction demanded. Where the company's legacy Cobra Acquisitions unit had built its reputation on storm-response and grid-restoration speed in Puerto Rico, 5 Star brought a different capability profile: planned, precision electrical infrastructure for facilities where uptime tolerances measured in nines and power densities were climbing past 50 kilowatts per rack.

The AI buildout provided a structural tailwind that was difficult to overstate from a contractor's standpoint. Hyperscaler and co-location operators were committing to campuses of 100 megawatts, 200 megawatts, and beyond, each requiring coordinated utility interconnection work, on-site medium-voltage distribution networks, and substation construction that could absorb years of specialised labour. For a contractor with 5 Star's size and regional footprint, the question entering 2026 was not whether demand existed but whether the company could scale its workforce, equipment fleet, and project management depth rapidly enough to capture meaningful share without margin-destroying execution risk.

The competitive field was formidable. [Quanta Services](https://investors.quantaservices.com), with its $22 billion-plus annual revenue base and decade-long relationships with investor-owned utilities, could mobilise linemen crews and substation engineering teams at a scale Mammoth could not match in a head-to-head bid. [MYR Group](https://ir.myrgroup.com), [MasTec](https://ir.mastec.com), and [Primoris Services](https://ir.primoris.com) occupied the mid-market tier between Quanta's dominance and smaller regional players, each pressing claims on data center electrical work through dedicated electrical construction divisions. Mammoth's addressable niche in that hierarchy ran toward projects where speed, regional presence, and flexibility on smaller total-contract-value work gave it an edge over the top-tier contractors who were rationing bandwidth toward nine-figure deals.

| Contractor | 2025 Revenue (approx.) | Primary data-center electrical positioning |
|---|---|---|
| Quanta Services | ~$23B | Large-scale utility interconnection, transmission |
| MasTec | ~$13B | Mid-market T&D, renewables tie-in |
| MYR Group | ~$4B | Commercial/industrial electrical, substation |
| Primoris Services | ~$7B | Industrial electrical, transmission |
| Mammoth / 5 Star | Sub-$1B | Regional data center electrical, storm-hardening |

The scale gap was not, in itself, a death sentence for the thesis. Infrastructure services is a fragmented industry where local contractor relationships, workforce retention in specific labour markets, and the ability to mobilise on compressed timelines can generate sustained gross margins without requiring a Quanta-scale balance sheet. What it did mean was that Mammoth's data center electrical story depended heavily on contract concentration risk remaining manageable and on the company avoiding the trap of taking on projects too large for its project controls infrastructure.

## PREPA: Three Resolution Scenarios

The Puerto Rico receivables dispute remained, as of the frozen snapshot date, the single largest variable affecting how investors priced the TUSK equity. Cobra Acquisitions had performed emergency T&D rebuild work across the island following Hurricane Maria in 2017, accruing hundreds of millions in billings to the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority. PREPA's subsequent bankruptcy filing converted what had been a straightforward accounts receivable into a creditor claim subject to restructuring proceedings, arbitration, and the cascading jurisdictional complexity of Title III of PROMESA.

The receivable had been carried on the balance sheet at a materially discounted value relative to the original billing, reflecting years of management conservatism about recovery timing and probability. Three resolution scenarios had crystallised by 2026.

In the **full-arbitration-recovery** scenario, the arbitration tribunal affirmed the bulk of Cobra's claimed receivables and PREPA's reorganisation plan provided for meaningful cash recovery. Even a partial recovery in the $150 million-plus range would represent a capital infusion relative to Mammoth's market capitalisation that would restructure the balance sheet entirely — eliminating leverage, funding capital expenditure for the infrastructure services expansion, and potentially enabling a return of capital to shareholders.

In the **negotiated-settlement** scenario — the one many restructuring analysts assigned the highest probability — both parties reached a discounted cash settlement to clear the claim from PREPA's reorganisation balance sheet ahead of any further plan confirmation proceedings. Precedent from other PREPA creditor classes suggested settlement values ranging from fifty to seventy cents on the dollar of allowed claims. The management of uncertainty, rather than maximum recovery, would drive timing.

In the **protracted-attrition** scenario, arbitration timelines extended further, PREPA's reorganisation stalled on broader political and bondholder dynamics, and Cobra's claim remained in limbo through 2027 or beyond. This outcome, while damaging to sentiment, did not affect Mammoth's operating cash generation from the infrastructure services pivot, but it would suppress the multiple at which the market was willing to value TUSK shares and constrain management's flexibility on capital allocation.

## Oilfield Services: The Managed Exit

The pressure pumping and oilfield services operations were, by early 2026, a business in deliberate terminal decline rather than active divestiture. Management had neither announced a formal sale process nor committed capital to fleet renewal, a posture that communicated the eventual endpoint without forcing a distressed transaction at trough cycle valuations. Natural sand proppant operations retained some residual cash generation given the low cost of legacy-mine assets, but incremental investment had effectively ceased. The segment's contribution to consolidated revenue had declined to a level where its operational complexity outweighed its financial significance.

The competitive logic for an exit was straightforward. Every dollar of management attention and capital diverted toward pressure pumping in a structurally oversupplied basin services market was a dollar unavailable for workforce recruitment, equipment procurement, and project development on the infrastructure services side — where returns on invested capital were structurally superior and demand visibility extended years rather than quarters.

## Capital Structure and Governance into 2030

Wexford Capital's legacy sponsorship shaped the governance overhang that institutional investors consistently flagged when evaluating TUSK. The Wexford-affiliated ownership concentration and board composition created an alignment dynamic that smaller public shareholders had long viewed with ambivalence: on one hand, a committed controlling investor with sector experience and a multi-year time horizon; on the other, a governance structure not optimised for the independent-board and executive-compensation benchmarks that index inclusion and institutional ownership thresholds demanded.

The capital structure thesis for 2026-2030 resolved, in most analyst frameworks, to a binary question about PREPA recovery timing. With a meaningful recovery, Mammoth had the financial capacity to fund an organic scale-up of the infrastructure services segment, pursue bolt-on acquisitions of regional electrical contractors, and improve governance metrics as part of a broader capital markets repositioning. Without near-term PREPA resolution, growth would remain constrained to what organic cash flow from infrastructure services could support — achievable, but slower, and subject to continued equity dilution risk if large project opportunities required balance sheet support.

The 2026-2030 horizon, viewed from the frozen snapshot date, presented Mammoth Energy as a company that had successfully identified the right market — electrical infrastructure for the AI buildout — but that carried the legacy weight of its own origin story in every financial line. The resolution of that tension, through arbitration outcome, oilfield exit, and workforce scale-up, would determine whether TUSK arrived at 2030 as a credible mid-market infrastructure contractor or as a cautionary tale about the cost of transformation left too long to the moment of crisis.

## PREPA Arbitration Reference

Cobra Acquisitions LLC performed emergency T&D restoration work across Puerto Rico following Hurricane Maria (2017). Billing disputes with the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority escalated into formal arbitration. PREPA's entry into Title III bankruptcy proceedings under PROMESA (the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act) extended resolution timelines materially. The disputed receivables — historically reported in the **$100 million-plus** range on Mammoth's consolidated balance sheet — represent the single largest binary variable in the company's asset valuation. As of the frozen snapshot date of 2026-05-23, the arbitration remained unresolved.
